clod.c: Clod Clod (klŏd), n. [OE. clodde, latter form of clot. See Clot.] 1. A lump or mass, especially of earth, turf, or clay. “Clods of a slimy substance.” Carew. “Clods of iron and brass.” Milton. “Clods of blood.” E. Fairfax.
Clod Clod (klŏd), v. i. To collect into clods, or into a thick mass; to coagulate; to clot; as, clodded gore. See Clot.
Clod Clod, v. t. 1. To pelt with clods. Jonson.

cloddish.c: Cloddish Clod"dish (?), a. Resembling clods; gross; low; stupid; boorish. Hawthorne.

cloddy.c: Cloddy Clod"dy (?), a. Consisting of clods; full of clods.

clodhopper.c: Clodhopper Clod"hop`per (?), n. A rude, rustic fellow.

clodhopping.c: Clodhopping Clod"hop`ping, a. Boorish; rude. C. Bronté.

clodpate.c: Clodpate Clod"pate` (?), n. A blockhead; a dolt.

clodpoll.c: Clodpoll Clod"poll` (?), n. [Clod + poll head.] A stupid fellow; a dolt. [Written also clodpole.] Shak.

cloff.c: Cloff Cloff (klŏf; 115), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] Formerly an allowance of two pounds in every three hundred weight after the tare and tret are subtracted; now used only in a general sense, of small deductions from the original weight. [Written also clough.] McCulloch.

clog.c: Clog Clog (klŏg), n. [OE. clogge clog, Scot. clag, n., a clot, v., to to obstruct, cover with mud or anything adhesive; prob. of the same origin as E. clay.] 1. That which hinders or impedes motion; hence, an encumbrance, restraint, or impediment, of any kind.
Clog Clog, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Clogged (klŏgd); p. pr. & vb. n. Clogging.] 1. To encumber or load, especially with something that impedes motion; to hamper.
Clog Clog, v. i. 1. To become clogged; to become loaded or encumbered, as with extraneous matter.

clogginess.c: Clogginess Clog"gi*ness (?), n. The state of being clogged.

clogging.c: Clogging Clog"ging, n. Anything which clogs. Dr. H. More.

cloggy.c: Cloggy Clog"gy (?), a. Clogging, or having power to clog.

cloisonne.c: Cloisonne ‖Cloi`son*né (?), a. [F., partitioned, fr. cloison a partition.] Inlaid between partitions: -- said of enamel when the lines which divide the different patches of fields are composed of a kind of metal wire secured to the ground; as distinguished from champlevé enamel, in which the ground is engraved or scooped out to receive the enamel. S. Wells Williams.

cloister.c: Cloister Clois"ter (?), n. [OF. cloistre, F. cloître, L. claustrum, pl. claustra, bar, bolt, bounds, fr. claudere, clausum, to close. See Close, v. t., and cf. Claustral.]
Cloister Clois"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cloistered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cloistering.] To confine in, or as in, a cloister; to seclude from the world; to immure.

cloistered.c: Cloistered Clois"tered (?), a. 1. Dwelling in cloisters; solitary. “Cloistered friars and vestal nuns.” Hudibras.

cloisterer.c: Cloisterer Clois"ter*er (?), n. [Cf. OF. cloistier.] One belonging to, or living in, a cloister; a recluse.

cloistral.c: Cloistral Clois"tral (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or confined in, a cloister; recluse. [Written also cloisteral.]

clomben.c: Clomben Clomb { Clomb (?), Clomb"en (?), } imp. & p. p. of Climb (for climbed). [Obs.]

clonic.c: Clonic Clon"ic (?), a. [Gr. klo`nos a violent, confused motion; cf. F. clonique.] (Med.) Having an irregular, convulsive motion. Dunglison.

clonus.c: Clonus ‖Clo"nus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. klo`nos violent, confused motion.] (Med.) A series of muscular contractions due to sudden stretching of the muscle, -- a sign of certain neuropathies.

cloom.c: Cloom Cloom (?), v. t. [A variant of clam to clog.] To close with glutinous matter. [Obs.] Mortimer.

cloop.c: Cloop Cloop (?), n. [An onomatopœia.] The sound made when a cork is forcibly drawn from a bottle. “The cloop of a cork wrenched from a bottle.” Thackeray.

cloot.c: Cloot Cloot (?), n. [Cf. G. dial. kleuzen to split.] (Scot. & Dial. Eng.) 1. One of the divisions of a cleft hoof, as in the ox; also, the whole hoof.

clootie.c: Clootie Cloot"ie (?), n. (Scot. & Dial. Eng.) 1. A little hoof.

close.c: Close Close (klōz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Closed (klōzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Closing.] [From OF. & F. clos, p. p. of clore to close, fr. L. claudere; akin to G. schliessen to shut, and to E. clot, cloister, clavicle, conclude, sluice. Cf. Clause, n.] 1. To stop, or fill up, as an opening; to shut; as, to close the eyes; to close a door.
Close Close, v. i. 1. To come together; to unite or coalesce, as the parts of a wound, or parts separated.
Close Close (?), n. 1. The manner of shutting; the union of parts; junction. [Obs.]

Close Close (? or?), n. [OF. & F. clos an inclosure, fr. clos, p. p. of clore. See Close, v. t.] 1. An inclosed place; especially, a small field or piece of land surrounded by a wall, hedge, or fence of any kind; -- specifically, the precinct of a cathedral or abbey.
Close Close (klōs), a. [Compar. Closer (klō"sẽr); superl. Closest.] [Of. & F. clos, p. p. of clore. See Close, v. t.] 1. Shut fast; closed; tight; as, a close box.
Close Close (klōs), adv. 1. In a close manner.

closebarred.c: Close-barred Close"-barred` (?), a. Firmly barred or closed.

closebodied.c: Close-bodied Close"-bod`ied (?), a. Fitting the body exactly; setting close, as a garment. Ayliffe.

closefights.c: Close-fights Close"-fights` (?), n. pl. (Naut.) Barriers with loopholes, formerly erected on the deck of a vessel to shelter the men in a close engagement with an enemy's boarders; -- called also close quarters. [Obs.]

closefisted.c: Closefisted Close"fist`ed (?), a. Covetous; niggardly. Bp. Berkeley. “Closefisted contractors.” Hawthorne.

closehanded.c: Closehanded Close"hand`ed (?), a. Covetous; penurious; stingy; closefisted. -- Close"hand`ed*ness, n.

closehauled.c: close-hauled Closehauled Close"hauled`, close-hauled (?), a. (Naut.) Under way and moving as nearly as possible toward the direction from which the wind blows; having the sails trimmed for sailing as close to the wind as possible; -- said of a sailing vessel.

closely.c: Closely Close"ly, adv. 1. In a close manner.

closemouthed.c: Closemouthed Close"mouthed` (?), a. Cautious in speaking; secret; wary; uncommunicative.

closen.c: Closen Clos"en (?), v. t. To make close. [R.]

closeness.c: Closeness Close"ness, n. The state of being close.

closer.c: Closer Clos"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, closes; specifically, a boot closer. See under Boot.

closereefed.c: Closereefed Close"reefed` (?), a. (Naut.) Having all the reefs taken in; -- said of a sail.

closestool.c: Close-stool Close"-stool` (?), n. A utensil to hold a chamber vessel, for the use of the sick and infirm. It is usually in the form of a box, with a seat and tight cover.

closet.c: Closet Clos"et (?), n. [OF. closet little inclosure, dim. of clos. See Close an inclosure.] 1. A small room or apartment for retirement; a room for privacy.
Closet Clos"et, v. t. [imp. & p. p.Closeted p. pr. & vb. n. Closeting.] 1. To shut up in, or as in, a closet; to conceal. [R.]

closetongued.c: Close-tongued Close"-tongued` (?), a. Closemouthed; silent. “Close-tongued treason.” Shak.

closh.c: Closh Closh (klŏsh), n. [CF. F. clocher to limp, halt.] A disease in the feet of cattle; laminitis. Crabb.
Closh Closh, n. [CF. D. klossen to play at bowls.] The game of ninepins. [Obs.] Halliwell.

closure.c: Closure Clo"sure (klō"zhur; 135), n. [Of. closure, L. clausura, fr. clauedere to shut. See Close, v. t.] 1. The act of shutting; a closing; as, the closure of a chink.

clot.c: Clot Clot (klŏt), n. [OE. clot, clodde, clod; akin to D. kloot ball, G. kloss clod, dumpling, klotz block, Dan. klods, Sw. klot bowl, globe, klots block; cf. AS. clāte bur. Cf. Clod, n., Clutter to clot.] A concretion or coagulation; esp. a soft, slimy, coagulated mass, as of blood; a coagulum. “Clots of pory gore.” Addison.
Clot Clot, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Clotted; p. pr. & vb. n. Clotting.] To concrete, coagulate, or thicken, as soft or fluid matter by evaporation; to become a clot or clod.
Clot Clot, v. t. To form into, or cover with, clots; to cause to coagulate; to make into a slimy mass.

clotbur.c: Clotbur Clot"bur` (klŏt"bûr`), n. [Cf. Clote.] 1. The burdock. [Prov. Engl.] Prior.

clote.c: Clote Clote (klōt), n. [AS. clāte: cf. G. klette.] The common burdock; the clotbur. [Obs.] Wyclif.

cloth.c: Cloth Cloth (klŏth; 115), n.; pl. Cloths (klŏthz; 115), except in the sense of garments, when it is Clothes (klōthz or klōz). [OE. clath cloth, AS. clāþ cloth, garment; akin to D. kleed, Icel. klæði, Dan. klæde, cloth, Sw. kläde, G. kleid garment, dress.] 1. A fabric made of fibrous material (or sometimes of wire, as in wire cloth); commonly, a woven fabric of cotton, woolen, or linen, adapted to be made into garments; specifically, woolen fabrics, as distinguished from all others.

clothe.c: Clothe Clothe (klōth), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Clothed (klōthd) or Clad (klăd); p. pr. & vb. n. Clothing.] [OE. clathen, clothen, clethen, AS. clāðian, clǣðan. See Cloth.] 1. To put garments on; to cover with clothing; to dress.
Clothe Clothe (?), v. i. To wear clothes. [Poetic]

clothes.c: Clothes Clothes (klōthz or klōz; 277), n. pl. [From Cloth.] 1. Covering for the human body; dress; vestments; vesture; -- a general term for whatever covering is worn, or is made to be worn, for decency or comfort.

clotheshorse.c: Clotheshorse Clothes"horse` (klōz"hôrs`), n. 1. A frame to hang clothes on.

clothesline.c: Clothesline Clothes"line` (klōz"līn`), n. A rope or wire on which clothes are hung to dry.

clothespin.c: Clothespin Clothes"pin` (? or?), n. A forked piece of wood or plastic, or a small device with a spring clamp, used for fastening clothes on a line.

clothespress.c: Clothespress Clothes"press` (?), n. A receptacle for clothes.

clothier.c: Clothier Cloth"ier (?), n. 1. One who makes cloths; one who dresses or fulls cloth. Hayward.

clothing.c: Clothing Cloth"ing (?), n. 1. Garments in general; clothes; dress; raiment; covering.

clotted.c: Clotted Clot"ted (?), a. Composed of clots or clods; having the quality or form of a clot; sticky; slimy; foul. “The clotted glebe.” J. Philips.

clotter.c: Clotter Clot"ter (?), v. i. [From Clot.] To concrete into lumps; to clot. [Obs.] “Clottered blood.” Chapman.

clotty.c: Clotty Clot"ty (?), a. [From Clot, n.] Full of clots, or clods. “Clotty matter.” Harvey.

cloud.c: Cloud Cloud (kloud), n. [Prob. fr. AS. clūd a rock or hillock, the application arising from the frequent resemblance of clouds to rocks or hillocks in the sky or air.] 1. A collection of visible vapor, or watery particles, suspended in the upper atmosphere.
Cloud Cloud (kloud), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Clouded; p. pr. & vb. n. Clouding.] 1. To overspread or hide with a cloud or clouds; as, the sky is clouded.
Cloud Cloud, v. i. To grow cloudy; to become obscure with clouds; -- often used with up.

cloudage.c: Cloudage Cloud"age (?), n. Mass of clouds; cloudiness. [R.]

cloudberry.c: Cloudberry Cloud"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) A species of raspberry (Rubus Chamæmerous) growing in the northern regions, and bearing edible, amber-colored fruit.

cloudbuilt.c: Cloud-built Cloud"-built (?), a. Built of, or in, the clouds; airy; unsubstantial; imaginary. Cowper.

cloudburst.c: Cloud-burst Cloud"-burst` (?), n. A sudden copious rainfall, as if the whole cloud had been precipitated at once.

cloudcapped.c: Cloud-capped Cloud"-capped` (?), a. Having clouds resting on the top or head; reaching to the clouds; as, cloud-capped mountains.

cloudcompeller.c: Cloud-compeller Cloud"-com*pel`ler (?), n. Cloud-gatherer; -- an epithet applied to Zeus. [Poetic.] Pope.

cloudily.c: Cloudily Cloud"i*ly (?), adv. In a cloudy manner; darkly; obscurely. Dryden.

cloudiness.c: Cloudiness Cloud"i*ness, n. The state of being cloudy.

clouding.c: Clouding Cloud"ing, n. 1. A mottled appearance given to ribbons and silks in the process of dyeing.

cloudless.c: Cloudless Cloud"less, a. Without a cloud; clear; bright.

cloudlet.c: Cloudlet Cloud"let (?), n. A little cloud. R. Browning.

cloudy.c: Cloudy Cloud"y (kloud"ŭ), a. [Compar. Cloudier (?); superl. Cloudiest.] [From Cloud, n.] 1. Overcast or obscured with clouds; clouded; as, a cloudy sky.

clough.c: Clough Clough (?), n. [OE. clough, cloghe, clou, clewch, AS. (assumed) clōh, akin to G. klinge ravine.] 1. A cleft in a hill; a ravine; a narrow valley. Nares.
Clough Clough (?; 115), n. (Com.) An allowance in weighing. See Cloff.

clout.c: Clout Clout (klout), n. [AS. clūt a little cloth, piece of metal; cf. Sw. klut, Icel. klūtr a kerchief, or W. clwt a clout, Gael. clud.] 1. A cloth; a piece of cloth or leather; a patch; a rag.

Clout Clout, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Clouted; p. pr. & vb. n. Clouting.] [OE. clutien. clouten, to patch. See Clout, n.] 1. To cover with cloth, leather, or other material; to bandage; patch, or mend, with a clout.

clouterly.c: Clouterly Clout"er*ly (?), a. [From Clout, n.] Clumsy; awkward. [Obs.]

clove.c: Clove Clove (?), imp. of Cleave. Cleft. Spenser.
Clove Clove, n. [D. kloof. See Cleave, v. t.] A cleft; a gap; a ravine; -- rarely used except as part of a proper name; as, Kaaterskill Clove; Stone Clove.

Clove Clove, n. [OE. clow, fr. F. clou nail, clou de girofle a clove, lit. nail of clove, fr. L. clavus nail, perh. akin to clavis key, E. clavicle. The clove was so called from its resemblance to a nail. So in D. kruidnagel clove, lit. herb-nail or spice-nail. Cf. Cloy.] A very pungent aromatic spice, the unexpanded flower bud of the clove tree (Eugenia aromatica syn. Caryophullus aromatica), a native of the Molucca Isles.

Clove Clove, n. [AS. clufe an ear of corn, a clove of garlic; cf. cleófan to split, E. cleave.] 1. (Bot.) One of the small bulbs developed in the axils of the scales of a large bulb, as in the case of garlic.

cloven.c: Cloven Clo"ven (klō"v'n), p. p. & a. from Cleave, v. t.

clovenhoofed.c: Cloven-hoofed Cloven-footed { Clo"ven-foot`ed (?), Clo"ven-hoofed` (?) }, a. Having the foot or hoof divided into two parts, as the ox.

clover.c: Clover Clo"ver (klō"vẽr), n. [OE. claver, clover, AS. clǣfre; akin to LG. & Dan. klever, D. klaver, G. klee, Sw. klöfver.] (Bot.) A plant of different species of the genus Trifolium; as the common red clover, Trifolium pratense, the white, Trifolium repens, and the hare's foot, Trifolium arvense.

clovered.c: Clovered Clo"vered (?), a. Covered with growing clover.

clowegilofre.c: Clowe-gilofre Clowe"-gi*lof`re (?), n. [See 3d Clove, and Gillyflower.] Spice clove. [Obs.] Chaucer.

clown.c: Clown Clown (kloun), n. [Cf. Icel. klunni a clumsy, boorish fellow, North Fries. klönne clown, dial. Sw. klunn log, Dan. klunt log, block, and E. clump, n.] 1. A man of coarse nature and manners; an awkward fellow; an ill-bred person; a boor. Sir P. Sidney.
Clown Clown, v. i. To act as a clown; -- with it. [Obs.]

clownage.c: Clownage Clown"age (?), n. Behavior or manners of a clown; clownery. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

clownish.c: Clownish Clown"ish, a. Of or resembling a clown, or characteristic of a clown; ungainly; awkward. “Clownish hands.” Spenser. “Clownish mimic.” Prior.

clownishness.c: Clownishness Clown"ish*ness, n. The manners of a clown; coarseness or rudeness of behavior.

cloy.c: Cloy Cloy (kloi), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cloyed (kloid); p. pr. & vb. n. Cloying.] [OE. cloer to nail up, F. clouer, fr. OF. clo nail, F. clou, fr. L. clavus nail. Cf. 3d Clove.] 1. To fill or choke up; to stop up; to clog. [Obs.]

cloyless.c: Cloyless Cloy"less, a. That does not cloy. Shak.

club.c: Club Club (klŭb), n. [Cf. Icel. klubba, klumba, club, klumbufōir a clubfoot, SW. klubba club, Dan. klump lump, klub a club, G. klumpen clump, kolben club, and E. clump.] 1. A heavy staff of wood, usually tapering, and wielded with the hand; a weapon; a cudgel.
Club Club (klŭb), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Clubbed (klŭbd); p. pr. & vb. n. Clubbing.] 1. To beat with a club.
Club Club (?), v. i. 1. To form a club; to combine for the promotion of some common object; to unite.

clubbable.c: Clubbable Club"ba*ble (?), a. Suitable for membership in a club; sociable. [Humorous.] [Also spelled clubable.] G. W. Curtis.

clubmoss.c: clubmoss club moss club" moss`, clubmoss n. (Bot.) a primitive evergreen mosslike plant with spores in club-shaped strobiles, much used in winter decoration. The best known species is Lycopodium clavatum, but other Lycopodia are often called by this name. The spores form a highly inflammable powder.

clubbed.c: Clubbed Clubbed (?), a. Shaped like a club; grasped like, or used as, a club. Skelton.

clubbist.c: Clubbist Club"bist (?), n. A member of a club; a frequenter of clubs. [R.] Burke.

clubfist.c: Clubfist Club"fist` (?), n. 1. A large, heavy fist.

clubfisted.c: Clubfisted Club"fist`ed, a. Having a large fist. Howell.

clubfoot.c: Clubfoot Club"foot (?), n. [Club + foot.] (Med.) A short, variously distorted foot; also, the deformity, usually congenital, which such a foot exhibits; talipes.

clubhand.c: Clubhand Club"hand` (?), n. (Med.) A short, distorted hand; also, the deformity of having such a hand.

clubhaul.c: Clubhaul Club"haul` (?), v. t. (Naut.) To put on the other tack by dropping the lee anchor as soon as the wind is out of the sails (which brings the vessel's head to the wind), and by cutting the cable as soon as she pays off on the other tack. Clubhauling is attempted only in an exigency.

clubhouse.c: Clubhouse Club"house` (?), n. A house occupied by a club.

clubroom.c: Clubroom Club"room` (?), n. The apartment in which a club meets. Addison.

clubrush.c: Club-rush Club"-rush` (?), n. (Bot.) A rushlike plant, the reed mace or cat-tail, or some species of the genus Scirpus. See Bulrush.

clubshaped.c: Club-shaped Club"-shaped (?), a. Enlarged gradually at the end, as the antennæ of certain insects.

cluck.c: Cluck Cluck (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Clucked (?); p pr. & vb. n. Clucking.] [AS. cloccian; cf. D. klokken, G. glucken, glucksen, LG. klukken, Dan. klukke; all prob. of imitative origin.] To make the noise, or utter the call, of a brooding hen. Ray.
Cluck Cluck, v. t. To call together, or call to follow, as a hen does her chickens.
Cluck Cluck, n. 1. The call of a hen to her chickens.

clucking.c: Clucking Cluck"ing, n. The noise or call of a brooding hen.

clumber.c: Clumber Clum"ber (klŭm"bẽr), n. [Named from the estate of the Duke of Newcastle.] (Zool.) A kind of field spaniel, with short legs and stout body, which, unlike other spaniels, hunts silently.

clump.c: Clump Clump (klŭmp), n. [Cf. D. klomp lump, G. klump, klumpen, Dan. klump, Sw. klump; perh. akin to L. globus, E. globe. Cf. Club.] 1. An unshaped piece or mass of wood or other substance.
Clump Clump, v. t. To arrange in a clump or clumps; to cluster; to group. Blackmore.
Clump Clump, v. i. To tread clumsily; to clamp. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

clumper.c: Clumper Clump"er (?), v. t. [Cf. G. klümpern to clod. See Clump, n.] To form into clumps or masses. [Obs.]

clumps.c: Clumps Clumps (?), n. A game in which questions are asked for the purpose of enabling the questioners to discover a word or thing previously selected by two persons who answer the questions; -- so called because the players take sides in two “clumps” or groups, the “clump” which guesses the word winning the game.

clumpy.c: Clumpy Clump"y (?), a. [From Clump, n.] Composed of clumps; massive; shapeless. Leigh Hunt.

clumsily.c: Clumsily Clum"si*ly (?), adv. In a clumsy manner; awkwardly; as, to walk clumsily.

clumsiness.c: Clumsiness Clum"si*ness, n. The quality of being clumsy.

clumsy.c: Clumsy Clum"sy (?), a. [Compar. Clumsier (?); superl. Clumsiest.] [OE. clumsed benumbed, fr. clumsen to be benumbed; cf. Icel. klumsa lockjaw, dial. Sw. klummsen benumbed with cold. Cf. 1st Clam, and 1st Clamp.] 1. Stiff or benumbed, as with cold. [Obs.]

clunch.c: Clunch Clunch (?), n. [Perh. fr. clinch to make fast] 1. (Mining) Indurated clay. See Bind, n., 3.

clung.c: Clung Clung (?), imp. & p. p. of Cling.
Clung Clung, a. [Prop. p. p. fr. OE. clingen to wither. See Cling, v. i.] Wasted away; shrunken. [Obs.]

cluniac.c: Cluniac Clu"ni*ac (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) A monk of the reformed branch of the Benedictine Order, founded in 912 at Cluny (or Clugny) in France. -- Also used as a.

clupeoid.c: Clupeoid Clu"pe*oid (?), a. [L.clupea a kind of fish, NL., generic name of the herring + -oid.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Herring family.

cluster.c: Cluster Clus"ter (klŭs"tẽr), n. [AS. cluster, clyster; cf. LG. kluster (also Sw. & Dan. klase a cluster of grapes, D. klissen to be entangled?.)] 1. A number of things of the same kind growing together; a bunch.
Cluster Clus"ter, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Clustered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Clustering.] To grow in clusters or assemble in groups; to gather or unite in a cluster or clusters.
Cluster Clus"ter, v. t. To collect into a cluster or clusters; to gather into a bunch or close body.

clustery.c: Clustery Clus"ter*y (?), a. [From Cluster, n.] Growing in, or full of, clusters; like clusters. Johnson.

clutch.c: Clutch Clutch (klŭch; 224), n. [OE. cloche, cloke, claw, Scot. clook, cleuck, also OE. cleche claw, clechen, cleken, to seize; cf. AS. gelæccan (where ge- is a prefix) to seize. Cf. Latch a catch.] 1. A gripe or clinching with, or as with, the fingers or claws; seizure; grasp. “The clutch of poverty.” Cowper.

Clutch Clutch, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Clutched (klŭcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Clutching.] [OE. clucchen. See Clutch, n.] 1. To seize, clasp, or grip with the hand, hands, or claws; -- often figuratively; as, to clutch power.
Clutch Clutch, v. i. 1. To reach (at something) as if to grasp; to catch or snatch; -- often followed by at.

clutter.c: Clutter Clut"ter (?), n. [Cf. W. cludair heap, pile, cludeirio to heap.] 1. A confused collection; hence, confusion; disorder; as, the room is in a clutter.

Clutter Clut"ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cluttered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cluttering.] To crowd together in disorder; to fill or cover with things in disorder; to throw into disorder; to disarrange; as, to clutter a room.
Clutter Clut"ter, v. i. To make a confused noise; to bustle.
Clutter Clut"ter, v. t. [From Clod, n.] To clot or coagulate, as blood. [Obs.] Holland.

clydesdale.c: Clydesdale Clydes"dale (?), n. One of a breed of heavy draft horses originally from Clydesdale, Scotland. They are about sixteen hands high and usually brown or bay.
Clydesdale terrier Clydesdale terrier. One of a breed of small silky-haired terriers related to, but smaller than, the Skye terrier, having smaller and perfectly erect ears.

clypeastroid.c: Clypeastroid Clyp`e*as"troid (?), a. [NL. Clypeaster (L. clupeus shield + aster star) + -oid.] (Zool.) Like or related to the genus Clupeaster; -- applied to a group of flattened sea urchins, with a rosette of pores on the upper side.

clypeate.c: Clypeate Clyp"e*ate (?), a. [L. clupeatus, p. p. of clupeare to arm with a shield, fr. clupeus, clipeus shield.] 1. (Bot.) Shaped like a round buckler or shield; scutate.

clypeiform.c: Clypeiform Clyp"e*i*form` (?), a. [L. clupeus shield + -form.] Shield-shaped; clypeate.

clypeus.c: Clypeus ‖Clyp"e*us (?), n.; pl. Clypei (#). [L., a shield.] (Zool.) The frontal plate of the head of an insect.

clysmian.c: Clysmian Clys"mi*an (?), a. [Gr.? a place washed by the waves, fr.?. See Clyster.] Connected with, or related to, the deluge, or to a cataclysm; as, clysmian changes. Smart.

clyster.c: Clyster Clys"ter (?), n. [L., fr. G.?. fr.? to wash off or out; akin to Goth. hlūtrs pure, G. lauter: cf. F. clystère] (Med.) A liquid injected into the lower intestines by means of a syringe; an injection; an enema.

clytie.c: Clytie knot Cly"tie knot (?). In hair dressing, a loose, low coil at the back of the head, like the knot on the head of the bust of Clytie by G. F. Watts.

cnemial.c: Cnemial Cne"mi*al (?), a. [Gr.? the tibia.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the shin bone.

cnida.c: Cnida ‖Cni"da (nī"dȧ), n.; pl. Cnidæ (nī"dē). [NL., fr. Gr. kni`dh nettle, sea nettle.] (Zool.) One of the peculiar stinging cells found in Cœlenterata; a nematocyst; a lasso cell.

cnidaria.c: Cnidaria ‖Cni*da"ri*a (nĭ*dā"rĭ*ȧ), n. pl. [NL. See Cnida.] (Zool.) A comprehensive group equivalent to the true Cœlenterata, i. e., exclusive of the sponges. They are so named from presence of stinging cells (cnidae) in the tissues. See Coelenterata.

cnidoblast.c: Cnidoblast Cni"do*blast (?), n. [Cnida + -blast.] (Zool.) One of the cells which, in the Cœlenterata, develop into cnidæ.

cnidocil.c: Cnidocil Cni"do*cil (?), n. [Cnida + cilium eyelash.] (Zool.) The fine filiform process of a cnidoblast.

co.c: Co- Co- (ko-). A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coacervate.c: Coacervate Co`a*cer"vate (?), a. [L. coacervatus, p. p. of coacervare to heap up; co- + acervare. See Acervate.] Raised into a pile; collected into a crowd; heaped. [R.] Bacon.
Coacervate Co`a*cer"vate (?), v. t. To heap up; to pile. [R.]

coacervation.c: Coacervation Co*ac`er*va"tion (?), n. [L. coacervatio.] A heaping together. [R.] Bacon.

coach.c: Coach Coach (kōch; 224), n. [F. coche, fr. It. cocchio, dim. of cocca little boat, fr. L. concha mussel, mussel shell, Gr.?, akin to Skr. çankha. Cf. Conch, Cockboat, Cockle.] 1. A large, closed, four-wheeled carriage, having doors in the sides, and generally a front and back seat inside, each for two persons, and an elevated outside seat in front for the driver.
Coach Coach, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coached (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coaching.] 1. To convey in a coach. Pope.
Coach Coach, v. i. To drive or to ride in a coach; -- sometimes used with it. [Colloq.] “Coaching it to all quarters.” E. Waterhouse.

coachbox.c: Coachbox Coach"box` (?). The seat of a coachman.

coachdog.c: Coachdog Coach"dog` (?; 115). (Zool.) One of a breed of dogs trained to accompany carriages; the Dalmatian dog.

coachfellow.c: Coachfellow Coach"fel`low (?), n. One of a pair of horses employed to draw a coach; hence (Fig.), a comrade. Shak.

coachman.c: Coachman Coach"man (?), n.; pl. Coachmen (#). 1. A man whose business is to drive a coach or carriage.

coachmanship.c: Coachmanship Coach"man*ship (?), n. Skill in driving a coach.

coachwhip.c: Coachwhip snake Coach"whip` snake" (?). (Zool.) A large, slender, harmless snake of the southern United States (Masticophis flagelliformis).

coact.c: Coact Co*act" (?), v. t. [L. coactare, intens. fr. cogere, coactum, to force. See Cogent.] To force; to compel; to drive. [Obs.]
Coact Co*act", v. i. [Pref. co- + act, v. i.] To act together; to work in concert; to unite. [Obs.]

coaction.c: Coaction Co*ac"tion (?), n. [L. coactio.] Force; compulsion, either in restraining or impelling. Sojth.

coactive.c: Coactive Co*ac"tive (?), a. [In sense 1, fr. 1st Coact; in sense 2, fr. 2d Coact.] 1. Serving to compel or constrain; compulsory; restrictive.

coactively.c: Coactively Co*ac"tive*ly, adv. In a coactive manner.

coadaptation.c: Coadaptation Co*ad`ap*ta"tion (?), n. Mutual adaption. R. Owen.

coadapted.c: Coadapted Co`a*dapt"ed (?), a. Adapted one to another; as, coadapted pulp and tooth. R. Owen.

coadjument.c: Coadjument Co*ad"ju*ment (?), n. Mutual help; cooperation. [R.] Johnson.

coadjust.c: Coadjust Co`ad*just" (?), v. t. To adjust by mutual adaptations. R. Owen.

coadjutant.c: Coadjutant Co*ad"ju*tant (?), a. Mutually assisting or operating; helping. J. Philips.
Coadjutant Co*ad"ju*tant, n. An assistant. R. North.

coadjutive.c: Coadjutive Co*ad"ju*tive (?), a. Rendering mutual aid; coadjutant. Feltham.

coadjutor.c: Coadjutor Co`ad*ju"tor (?), n. [L. See Co-, and Aid.] 1. One who aids another; an assistant; a coworker.

coadjutorship.c: Coadjutorship Co`ad*ju"tor*ship, n. The state or office of a coadjutor; joint assistance. Pope.

coadjutrix.c: Coadjutrix Coadjutress { Co`ad*ju"tress (?), Co`ad*ju"trix (?), } n. A female coadjutor or assistant. Holland. Smollett.

coadjuvancy.c: Coadjuvancy Co*ad"ju*van*cy (?), n. Joint help; cooperation. Sir T. Browne.

coadunate.c: Coadunate Co*ad"u*nate (?; 135), a. [L. coadunatus, p. p. of coadunare to unite. See Adunation.] (Bot.) United at the base, as contiguous lobes of a leaf.

coadunation.c: Coadunation Co*ad`u*na"tion (?), n. [L. coadunatio.] Union, as in one body or mass; unity. Jer. Taylor.

coadunition.c: Coadunition Co*ad`u*ni"tion (?), n. [Pref. co- + pref. ad- + unition.] Coadunation. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

coadventure.c: Coadventure Co`ad*ven"ture (?; 135), n. An adventure in which two or more persons are partakers.
Coadventure Co`ad*ven"ture, v. i. To share in a venture. Howell.

coafforest.c: Coafforest Co`af*for"est (?), v. t. To convert into, or add to, a forest. Howell.

coag.c: Coag Coag (?), n. See Coak, a kind of tenon.

coagency.c: Coagency Co*a"gen*cy (?), n. Agency in common; joint agency or agent. Coleridge.

coagent.c: Coagent Co*a"gent (?), n. An associate in an act; a coworker. Drayton.

coagment.c: Coagment Co`ag*ment" (?), v. t. [L. coagmentare, fr. coagmentum a joining together, fr. cogere. See Cogent.] To join together. [Obs.] Glanvill.

coagmentation.c: Coagmentation Co*ag`men*ta"tion (?), n. [L. coagmentatio.] The act of joining, or the state of being joined, together; union. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

coagulability.c: Coagulability Co*ag`u*la*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being coagulable; capacity of being coagulated. Ure.

coagulable.c: Coagulable Co*ag"u*la*ble (?), a. Capable of being coagulated. Boyle.

coagulant.c: Coagulant Co*ag"u*lant (?), n. [L. coagulans, p. pr.] That which produces coagulation.

coagulate.c: Coagulate Co*ag"u*late (?), a. [L. coagulatus, p. p. of coagulare to coagulate, fr. coagulum means of coagulation, fr. cogere, coactum, to drive together, coagulate. See Cogent.] Coagulated. [Obs.] Shak.

Coagulate Co*ag"u*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coagulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coagulating (?).] To cause (a liquid) to change into a curdlike or semisolid state, not by evaporation but by some kind of chemical reaction; to curdle; as, rennet coagulates milk; heat coagulates the white of an egg.
Coagulate Co*ag"u*late, v. i. To undergo coagulation. Boyle.

coagulated.c: Coagulated Co*ag"u*la`ted (?), a. Changed into, or contained in, a coagulum or a curdlike mass; curdled.

coagulation.c: Coagulation Co*ag`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. coagulatio.] 1. The change from a liquid to a thickened, curdlike, insoluble state, not by evaporation, but by some kind of chemical reaction; as, the spontaneous coagulation of freshly drawn blood; the coagulation of milk by rennet, or acid, and the coagulation of egg albumin by heat. Coagulation is generally the change of an albuminous body into an insoluble modification.

coagulative.c: Coagulative Co*ag"u*la*tive (?), a. Having the power to cause coagulation; as, a coagulative agent. Boyle.

coagulator.c: Coagulator Co*ag"u*la`tor (?), n. That which causes coagulation. Hixley.

coagulatory.c: Coagulatory Co*ag"u*la*to*ry (?), a. Serving to coagulate; produced by coagulation; as, coagulatory effects. Boyle.

coagulum.c: Coagulum Co*ag"u*lum (?), n.; pl. Coagula (#). [L. See Coagulate, a.] The thick, curdy precipitate formed by the coagulation of albuminous matter; any mass of coagulated matter, as a clot of blood.

coaita.c: Coaita ‖Co*ai"ta (ko*äĭ"tȧ), n. (Zool.) The native name of certain South American monkeys of the genus Ateles, esp. Ateles paniscus. The black-faced coaita is Ateles ater. See Illustration in Appendix.

coak.c: Coak Coak, n. 1. (Carp.) A kind of tenon connecting the face of a scarfed timber with the face of another timber, or a dowel or pin of hard wood or iron uniting timbers. [Also spelt coag.]
Coak Coak, v. t. (Carp.) To unite, as timbers, by means of tenons or dowels in the edges or faces. Totten.

coal.c: Coal Coal (kōl), n. [AS. col; akin to D. kool, OHG. chol, cholo, G. kohle, Icel. kol, pl., Sw. kol, Dan. kul; cf. Skr. jval to burn. Cf. Kiln, Collier.] 1. A thoroughly charred, and extinguished or still ignited, fragment from wood or other combustible substance; charcoal.
Coal Coal, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coaled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coaling.] 1. To burn to charcoal; to char. [R.]
Coal Coal, v. i. To take in coal; as, the steamer coaled at Southampton.

Coal tar Coal" tar` (?). A thick, black, tarry liquid, obtained by the distillation of bituminous coal in the manufacture of illuminating gas; used for making printer's ink, black varnish, etc. It is a complex mixture from which many substances have been obtained, especially hydrocarbons of the benzene or aromatic series.
Coal works Coal" works (?). A place where coal is dug, including the machinery for raising the coal.

coalblack.c: Coal-black Coal"-black` (-blăk`), a. As black as coal; jet black; very black. Dryden.

coalesce.c: Coalesce Co`a*lesce" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Coalesced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coalescing.] [L. coalescere, coalitium; co- + alescere to grow up, incho. fr. alere to nourish. See Aliment, n.] 1. To grow together; to unite by growth into one body; as, the parts separated by a wound coalesce.

coalescence.c: Coalescence Co`a*les"cence (?), n. The act or state of growing together, as similar parts; the act of uniting by natural affinity or attraction; the state of being united; union; concretion.

coalescent.c: Coalescent Co`a*les"cent (?), a. [L. coalescens, p. pr.] Growing together; cohering, as in the organic cohesion of similar parts; uniting.

coalfish.c: Coalfish Coal"fish` (?), n. [Named from the dark color of the back.] (Zool.) (a) The pollock; -- called also, coalsey, colemie, colmey, coal whiting, etc. See Pollock. (b) The beshow or candlefish of Alaska. (c) The cobia.

coalgoose.c: Coalgoose Coal"goose` (?), n. (Zool.) The cormorant; -- so called from its black color.

coalite.c: Coalite Co"a*lite (?), v. i. [L. coalitus, p. p. of coalescere. See Coalesce.] To unite or coalesce. [Obs.]
Coalite Co"a*lite, v. t. To cause to unite or coalesce. [Obs.]

coalition.c: Coalition Co`a*li"tion (?), n. [LL. coalitio: cf. F. coalition. See Coalesce.] 1. The act of coalescing; union into a body or mass, as of separate bodies or parts; as, a coalition of atoms. Bentley.

coalitionist.c: Coalitionist Co`a*li"tion*ist, n. One who joins or promotes a coalition; one who advocates coalition.

coally.c: Co-ally Co`-al*ly" (?), n.; pl. Co-allies (#). A joint ally. Kent.

coalmeter.c: Coal-meter Coal"-me`ter (?), n. A licensed or official coal measurer in London. See Meter. Simmonds.

coalmouse.c: Coalmouse Coal"mouse` (?), n. (Zool.) A small species of titmouse, with a black head; the coletit.

coalpit.c: Coalpit Coal"pit` (?), n. 1. A pit where coal is dug.

coalsack.c: Coalsack Coal"sack` (?), n. [Coal + 2d sack.] (Astron.) Any one of the spaces in the Milky Way which are very black, owing to the nearly complete absence of stars; esp., the large space near the Southern Cross sometimes called the Black Magellanic Cloud.

coalwhipper.c: Coal-whipper Coal"-whip`per (?), n. One who raises coal out of the hold of a ship. [Eng.] Dickens.

coaly.c: Coaly Coal"y (?), a. [From Coal, n.] Pertaining to, or resembling, coal; containing coal; of the nature of coal.

coamings.c: Coamings Coam"ings (?), n. pl. [Cf. Comb a crest.] (Naut.) Raised pieces of wood of iron around a hatchway, skylight, or other opening in the deck, to prevent water from running bellow; esp. the fore-and-aft pieces of a hatchway frame as distinguished from the transverse head ledges. [Written also combings.]

coannex.c: Coannex Co`an*nex" (?), v. t. To annex with something else.

coaptation.c: Coaptation Co`ap*ta"tion (?), n. [L. coaptatio, fr. coaptare to fit together; co- + aptare. See Aptate.] The adaptation or adjustment of parts to each other, as of a broken bone or dislocated joint.

coarctate.c: Coarctate Coarct { Co*arct" (?), Co*arc"tate (?) }, v. t. [See Coarctate, a.] 1. To press together; to crowd; to straiten; to confine closely. [Obs.] Bacon.

Coarctate Co*arc"tate (?), a. [L. coarctatus, p. p. of coarctare to press together; co- + arctare to press together, from arctus, p. p. See Arctation.] (Zool.) Pressed together; closely connected; -- applied to insects having the abdomen separated from the thorax only by a constriction.

coarctation.c: Coarctation Co`arc*ta"tion (?), n. [L. coarctatio.] 1. Confinement to a narrow space. [Obs.] Bacon.

coarse.c: Coarse Coarse (kōrs), a. [Compar. Coarser (kōrs"ẽr); superl. Coarsest.] [As this word was anciently written course, or cours, it may be an abbreviation of of course, in the common manner of proceeding, common, and hence, homely, made for common domestic use, plain, rude, rough, gross, e. g., “Though the threads be course.” Gascoigne. See Course.]

coarsegrained.c: Coarse-grained Coarse"-grained` (kōrs"grānd`), a. Having a coarse grain or texture, as wood; hence, wanting in refinement.

coarsely.c: Coarsely Coarse"ly (kōrs"ly̆), adv. In a coarse manner; roughly; rudely; inelegantly; uncivilly; meanly.

coarsen.c: Coarsen Coars"en (kōrs"'n), v. t. To make coarse or vulgar; as, to coarsen one's character. [R.] Graham.

coarseness.c: Coarseness Coarse"ness (kōrs"nĕs), n. The quality or state of being coarse; roughness; inelegance; vulgarity; grossness; as, coarseness of food, texture, manners, or language. “The coarseness of the sackcloth.” Dr. H. More.

coarticulation.c: Coarticulation Co`ar*tic`u*la"tion (?), n. (Anat.) The union or articulation of bones to form a joint.

coast.c: Coast Coast (kōst), n. [OF. coste, F. côte, rib, hill, shore, coast, L. costa rib, side. Cf. Accost, v. t., Cutlet.] 1. The side of a thing. [Obs.] Sir I. Newton.

Coast Coast (kōst), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Coasted; p. pr. & vb. n. Coasting.] [OE. costien, costeien, costen, OF. costier, costoier, F. côtoyer, fr. Of. coste coast, F. côte. See Coast, n.] 1. To draw or keep near; to approach. [Obs.]
Coast Coast, v. t. 1. To draw near to; to approach; to keep near, or by the side of. [Obs.] Hakluyt.

Coast and Geodetic Survey Coast and Geodetic Survey. A bureau of the United States government charged with the topographic and hydrographic survey of the coast and the execution of belts of primary triangulation and lines of precise leveling in the interior. It now belongs to the Department of Commerce and Labor.

coastal.c: Coastal Coast"al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a coast.

coaster.c: Coaster Coast"er (?), n. 1. A vessel employed in sailing along a coast, or engaged in the coasting trade.

coasting.c: Coasting Coast"ing (?), a. Sailing along or near a coast, or running between ports along a coast.
Coasting Coast"ing, n. 1. A sailing along a coast, or from port to port; a carrying on a coasting trade.

coastways.c: Coastways Coastwise { Coast"wise` (-wīz`), Coast"ways` (?), } adv. By way of, or along, the coast; following a coastline; as, coastwise winds contributed to the storm.

coat.c: Coat Coat (kōt; 110), n. [OF. cote, F. cotte, petticoat, cotte d'armes coat of arms, cotte de mailles coat of mail, LL. cota, cotta, tunic, prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. chozzo coarse mantle, G. klotze, D. kot, hut, E. cot. Cf. Cot a hut.] 1. An outer garment fitting the upper part of the body; especially, such a garment worn by men.
Coat Coat (kōt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coated; p. pr. & vb. n. Coating.] 1. To cover with a coat or outer garment.

coatee.c: Coatee Coat*ee" (kot*ē"), n. A coat with short flaps.

coati.c: Coati Co*a"ti (ko*ä"te or ko*ā"tĭ), n. [From the native name: cf. F. coati.] (Zool.) A mammal of tropical America of the genus Nasua, allied to the raccoon, having a ringed tail but with a longer body, tail, and nose; -- called also coati mondi and coati mundi.

coating.c: Coating Coat"ing (kō"ĭng), n. 1. A coat or covering; a layer of any substance, as a cover or protection; as, the coating of a retort or vial.

coatless.c: Coatless Coat"less (?), a. Not wearing a coat; also, not possessing a coat.

coax.c: Coax Coax (kōks; 110), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coaxed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coaxing.] [Cf. OE. cokes fool, a person easily imposed upon, W. coeg empty, foolish; F. coquin knave, rogue.] To persuade by gentle, insinuating courtesy, flattering, or fondling; to wheedle; to soothe.
Coax Coax, n. A simpleton; a dupe. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

coaxation.c: Coaxation Co`ax*a"tion (?), n. [Gr.? the noise of frogs.] The act of croaking. [R] Dr. H. More.

coaxingly.c: Coaxingly Coax"ing*ly, adv. In a coaxing manner; by coaxing.

cob.c: Cob Cob (?), n. [Cf. AS. cop, copp, head, top, D. kop, G. kopf, kuppe, LL. cuppa cup (cf. E. brainpan), and also W. cob tuft, spider, cop, copa, top, summit, cobio to thump. Cf. Cop top, Cup, n.] 1. The top or head of anything. [Obs.] W. Gifford.
Cob Cob, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cobbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cobbing.] 1. To strike [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

cobaea.c: Cobaea Cobaea Co*bae"a, Co*bæ"a (ko*bē"ȧ), prop. n. [Named after D. Cobo, a Spanish botanist.] A genus of climbing plants, native of Mexico and South America. Cobaea scandens (called cup-and-saucer vine, monastery bells, or Mexican ivy) is a conservatory climber with large bell-shaped flowers.

cobalt.c: Cobalt Co"balt (kō"bŏlt; 277, 74), n. [G. kobalt, prob. fr. kobold, kobel, goblin, MHG. kobolt; perh. akin to G. koben pigsty, hut, AS. cofa room, cofgodas household gods, Icel. kofi hut. If so, the ending -old stands for older -walt, -wald, being the same as -ald in E. herald and the word would mean ruler or governor in a house, house spirit, the metal being so called by miners, because it was poisonous and troublesome. Cf. Kobold, Cove, Goblin.] 1. (Chem.) A tough, lustrous, reddish white metal of the iron group, not easily fusible, and somewhat magnetic. Atomic weight 59.1. Symbol Co.

cobaltic.c: Cobaltic Co*balt"ic (?; 74), a. [Cf. F. cobaltique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, cobalt; -- said especially of those compounds in which cobalt has higher valence; as, cobaltic oxide.

cobaltite.c: Cobaltite Cobaltine { Co"balt*ine (?), Co"balt*ite (?) } n. (Min.) A mineral of a nearly silver-white color, composed of arsenic, sulphur, and cobalt.

cobaltous.c: Cobaltous Co*balt"ous (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, cobalt; -- said esp. of cobalt compounds in which the metal has its lower valence.

cobbing.c: Cobbing Cob"bing (?), a. Haughty; purse-proud. See Cob, n., 2. [Obs.] Withals (1608).

cobble.c: Cobble Cob"ble (?), n. A fishing boat. See Coble.
Cobble Cob"ble, n. [From Cob a lump. See Cob, n., 9, and cf. Copple, Copplestone.] 1. A cobblestone. “Their slings held cobbles round.” Fairfax.

Cobble Cob"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cobbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cobbling (?).] [OF. cobler, copler, to join or knit together, couple, F. coupler, L. copulare to couple, join. Cf. Couple, n. & v. t.] 1. To make or mend coarsely; to patch; to botch; as, to cobble shoes. Shak. “A cobbled saddle.” Thackeray.

cobbler.c: Cobbler Cob"bler (?), n. 1. A mender of shoes. Addison.

cobblestone.c: Cobblestone Cob"ble*stone` (?), n. A large pebble; a rounded stone not too large to be handled; a small boulder; -- used for paving streets and for other purposes.

cobby.c: Cobby Cob"by (?), a. [From Cob, n.] 1. Headstrong; obstinate. [Obs.] Brockett.

cobelligerent.c: Cobelligerent Co`bel*lig"er*ent (?), a. Carrying on war in conjunction with another power.
Cobelligerent Co`bel*lig"er*ent, n. A nation or state that carries on war in connection with another.

cobia.c: Cobia Co"bi*a (?), n. (Zool.) An oceanic fish of large size (Elacate canada); the crabeater; -- called also bonito, cubbyyew, coalfish, and sergeant fish.

cobiron.c: Cobiron Cob"i`ron (?), n. [From Cob the top.] An andiron with a knob at the top. Bacon.

cobishop.c: Cobishop Co`bish"op (?), n. A joint or coadjutant bishop. Ayliffe.

coble.c: Coble Co"ble (?), n. [AS. cuopel; cf. W. ceubal skiff, ferryboat.] A flat-floored fishing boat with a lug sail, and a drop rudder extending from two to four feet below the keel. It was originally used on the stormy coast of Yorkshire, England.

cobnut.c: Cobnut Cob"nut` (?), n. 1. (Com.) A large roundish variety of the cultivated hazelnut.

cobourg.c: Cobourg Co"bourg (?), n. [Named from the town of Coburg in Germany.] A thin worsted fabric for women's dresses.

cobra.c: Cobra Co"bra, n. The cobra de capello.
Cobra de capello ‖Co"bra de ca*pel"lo (?). [Pg., serpent of the hood.] (Zool.) The hooded snake (Naia tripudians), a highly venomous serpent inhabiting India.Naja -->

cobswan.c: Cobswan Cob"swan` (?), n. A large swan. B. Jonson.

cobwall.c: Cobwall Cob"wall` (?), n. [Cob clay mixed with straw + wall.] A wall made of clay mixed with straw.

cobweb.c: Cobweb Cob"web` (?), n. [Cob a spider + web.] 1. The network spread by a spider to catch its prey.

cobwebbed.c: Cobwebbed Cob"webbed` (?), a. Abounding in cobwebs. “The cobwebbed cottage.” Young.

cobwebby.c: Cobwebby Cob"web`by (?), a. Abounding in cobwebs, or any fine web; resembling a cobweb.

cobwork.c: Cobwork Cob"work` (?), a. Built of logs, etc., laid horizontally, with the ends dovetailed together at the corners, as in a log house; in marine work, often surrounding a central space filled with stones; as, a cobwork dock or breakwater.

coca.c: Coca Co"ca (?), n. [Sp., fr. native name.] The dried leaf of a South American shrub (Erythroxylon Coca). In med., called Erythroxylon.

cocagne.c: Cocagne Coc*agne" (?), n. [F. cocagne, pays de cocagne; of uncertian origin, cf. Prov. F. couque cake, Catal. coca, L. coquere to cook; as if the houses in this country were covered with cakes. Cf. Cook, Cockney.] 1. An imaginary country of idleness and luxury.

cocaine.c: Cocaine Co"ca*ine (?), n. (Chem.) A powerful narcotic alkaloid, C17H21NO4, obtained from the leaves of coca. It is a bitter, white, crystalline substance, and is remarkable for producing local insensibility to pain. It is classified as addictive and is not available in the U. S. without a prescription, but is nevertheless one of the most widespread illegal drugs of abuse. It is used in several forms, including small pellets of free base, called crack. Most of the cacaine illegally used in the U.S. is imported.

cocainism.c: Cocainism Co*ca"in*ism (?), n. (Med.) A morbid condition produced by the habitual and excessive use of cocaine. -- Co*ca"in*ist, n.

cocainize.c: Cocainize Co*ca"in*ize (?), v. t. To treat or anæsthetize with cocaine. -- Co*ca`in*i*za"tion (#), n.

cocciferous.c: Cocciferous Coc*cif"er*ous (?), a. [L. coccum a berry + -ferous. See Coccus.] Bearing or producing berries; bacciferous; as, cocciferous trees or plants.

coccinella.c: Coccinella ‖Coc`ci*nel"la (?), n. [NL., fr. L. coccineus scarlet-colored. See Cochoneal.] (Zool.) A genus of small beetles of many species. They and their larvæ feed on aphids or plant lice, and hence are of great benefit to man. Also called ladybirds and ladybugs.

coccobacterium.c: Coccobacterium ‖Coc`co*bac*te"ri*um (?), n.; pl. Coccobacteria (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? a grain + NL. bacterium. So called from its round shape.] (Biol.) One of the round variety of bacteria, a vegetable organism, generally less than a thousandth of a millimeter in diameter.

coccolite.c: Coccolite Coc"co*lite (?), n. [Gr.? a grain, seed + -lite: cf. F. coccalite.] (Min.) A granular variety of pyroxene, green or white in color.

coccolith.c: Coccolith Coc"co*lith (?), n. [Gr.? a grain, seed + -lith.] (Biol.) One of a kind of minute, calcareous bodies, probably vegetable, often abundant in deep-sea mud.

coccosphere.c: Coccosphere Coc"co*sphere (?), n. [Gr.? a grain, seed + E. sphere.] (Biol.) A small, rounded, marine organism, capable of braking up into coccoliths.

coccosteus.c: Coccosteus ‖Coc*cos"te*us (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? grain, seed +? bone.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of Devonian ganoid fishes, having the broad plates about the head studded with berrylike tubercles.

cocculus.c: Cocculus Indicus ‖Coc"cu*lus In"di*cus (?), n. [NL. cocculus (dim. of L. coccum kermes berry) + L. Indicus of India.] (Bot.) The fruit or berry of the Anamirta Cocculus, a climbing plant of the East Indies. It is a poisonous narcotic and stimulant.

coccus.c: Coccus ‖Coc"cus (?), n.; pl. Cocci (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? grain, seed. See Cochineal.] 1. (Bot.) One of the separable carpels of a dry fruit.

coccygeal.c: Coccygeal Coc*cyg"e*al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the coccyx; as, the coccygeal vertebræ.

coccyx.c: Coccyx ‖Coc"cyx (?), n.; pl. L. Coccyges (#). [L., cuckoo, Gr.?, cuckoo, coccyx. So called from its resemblance to the beak of a cuckoo.] (Anat.) The end of the vertebral column beyond the sacrum in man and tailless monkeys. It is composed of several vertebræ more or less consolidated.

cochineal.c: Cochineal Coch"i*neal (kŏch"ĭ*nēl; 277), [Sp. cochinilla, dim. from L. coccineus, coccinus, scarlet, fr. coccum the kermes berry, G. ko`kkos berry, especially the kermes insect, used to dye scarlet, as the cochineal was formerly supposed to be the grain or seed of a plant, and this word was formerly defined to be the grain of the Quercus coccifera; but cf. also Sp. cochinilla wood louse, dim. of cochina sow, akin to F. cochon pig.] A dyestuff consisting of the dried bodies of females of the Coccus cacti, an insect native in Mexico, Central America, etc., and found on several species of cactus, esp. Opuntia cochinellifera.
Cochineal fig Coch"i*neal fig (?), (Bot.) A plant of Central and Southern America, of the Cactus family, extensively cultivated for the sake of the cochineal insect, which lives on it.

cochin.c: Cochin fowl Co"chin fowl` (?), (Zool.) A large variety of the domestic fowl, originally from Cochin China (Anam).

cochlea.c: Cochlea ‖Coch"le*a (kŏk"le*ȧ), n. [L., a snail, or snail shell, Gr. kochli`as a snail, fr. ko`chlos a shellfish with a spiral shell.] (Anat.) An appendage of the labyrinth of the internal ear, which is elongated and coiled into a spiral in mammals. See Ear.

cochlear.c: Cochlear Coch"le*ar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the cochlea.

cochleary.c: Cochleary Coch"le*a*ry (?), a. [L. cochlearum penfor snails (meaning formerly given, snail shell). See Cjchlea.] Same as Cochleate.

cochleated.c: Cochleated Cochleate { Coch"le*ate (?), Coch"le*a`ted (?), } a. [L. cochleatus spiral or screw-formed. See Cochlea.] Having the form of a snail shell; spiral; turbinated.

cock.c: Cock Cock (kŏk), n. [AS. coc; of unknown origin, perh. in imitation of the cry of the cock. Cf. Chicken.] 1. The male of birds, particularly of gallinaceous or domestic fowls.
Cock Cock (kŏk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cocked (kŏkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Cocking.] [Cf. Gael. coc to cock.] 1. To set erect; to turn up.
Cock Cock, v. i. To strut; to swagger; to look big, pert, or menacing. Addison.
Cock Cock, n. The act of cocking; also, the turn so given; as, a cock of the eyes; to give a hat a saucy cock.
Cock Cock, n. [It. cocca notch of an arrow.] 1. The notch of an arrow or crossbow.
Cock Cock, v. t. To draw the hammer of (a firearm) fully back and set it for firing.
Cock Cock, v. i. To draw back the hammer of a firearm, and set it for firing.
Cock Cock, n. [Cf. Icel. kökkr lump, Dan. kok heap, or E. cock to set erect.] A small concial pile of hay.
Cock Cock, v. t. To put into cocks or heaps, as hay.
Cock Cock, n. [Of. coque, F. coche, a small vessel, L. concha muscle shell, a vessel. See Coach, and cf. Cog a small boat.] A small boat.
Cock Cock, n. A corruption or disguise of the word God, used in oaths. [Obs.] “By cock and pie.” Shak.

cockade.c: Cockade Cock*ade" (?), n. [F. cocarble, fr. coquard vain, OF. coquart, fr. coq cock, prob. of imitative origin. The ornament is so named from its resemblance to the crest of a cock. Cf. Coquette.] A badge, usually in the form of a rosette, or knot, and generally worn upon the hat; -- used as an indication of military or naval service, or party allegiance, and in England as a part of the livery to indicate that the wearer is the servant of a military or naval officer.

cockaded.c: Cockaded Cock*ad"ed (?), a. Wearing a cockade. Young.

cockahoop.c: cock-a-hoop cock`-a-hoop" (?), a. Boastful; defiant; exulting. Also used adverbially.

cockal.c: Cockal Cock"al (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] 1. A game played with sheep's bones instead of dice. [Obs.]

cockaleekie.c: cock-a-leekie Cockaleekie Cock`a*leek"ie, cock-a-leekie (?), n. [From cock + leek.] A favorite soup in Scotland, made from a capon highly seasoned, and boiled with leeks and prunes; -- called also cocky-leeky.

cockamaroo.c: Cockamaroo Cock`a*ma*roo" (?), n. The Russian variety of bagatelle.

cockateel.c: Cockateel cockatiel cock"a*tiel, Cock"a*teel (?), n. (Zool.) A small gray and white Australian parrot (Leptolophus hollandicus, formerly Calopsitta Novæ-Hollandiæ) with a prominent crest; the male has bright yellow cheeks and crest, but the female has only a pale yellow in the face; -- it is so called from its note.

cockatoo.c: Cockatoo Cock`a*too" (kŏk`ȧ*tōo"), n. [Malayan kakatūa.] (Zool.) A bird of the Parrot family, of the subfamily Cacatuinæ, having a short, strong, and much curved beak, and the head ornamented with a crest, which can be raised or depressed at will. There are several genera and many species; as the broad-crested cockatoo (Plictolophus cristatus or Cacatua cristatus), the sulphur-crested (Cacatua galerita or Plictolophus galeritus), etc. The palm cockatoo or great black cockatoo of Australia is Probosciger aterrimus (formerly Microglossus aterrimus).

cockatrice.c: Cockatrice Cock"a*trice (-trīs; 277), n. [OF. cocatrice crocodile, F. cocatrix, cocatrice. The word is a corruption from the same source as E. crocodile, but was confused with cock the bird, F. coq, whence arose the fable that the animal was produced from a cock's egg. See Crocodile.]

cockbill.c: Cockbill Cock"bill (kŏk"bĭl`), v. t. [See Cock to set erect.] (Naut.) To tilt up one end of so as to make almost vertical; as, to cockbill the yards as a sign of mourning.

cockboat.c: Cockboat Cock"boat` (?), n. [See Cock a boat.] A small boat, esp. one used on rivers or near the shore.

cockchafer.c: Cockchafer Cock"chaf`er (?), n. [See Chafer the beetle.] (Zool.) A beetle of the genus Melolontha (esp. Melolontha vulgaris) and allied genera; -- called also May bug, chafer, or dorbeetle.

cockcrowing.c: Cockcrowing Cockcrow { Cock"crow (?), Cock"crow`ing, } n. The time at which cocks first crow; the early morning; the first light of day.

cocker.c: Cocker Cock"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cockered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cockering.] [OE. cokeren; cf. W. cocru to indulge, fondle, E. cock the bird, F. coqueliner to dandle (Cotgrave), to imitate the crow of a cock, to run after the girls, and E. cockle, v.] To treat with too great tenderness; to fondle; to indulge; to pamper.
Cocker Cock"er, n. [From Cock the bird.] 1. One given to cockfighting. [Obs.] Steele.

Cocker Cock"er, n. [OE. coker qyiver, boot, AS. cocer quiver; akin to G. köcher quiver, and perh. originally meaning receptacle, holder. Cf. Quiver (for arrows).] A rustic high shoe or half-boots. [Obs.] Drayton.

Cocker spaniel Cock"er span"iel. One of a breed of small or medium-sized spaniels kept for hunting or retrieving game or for household pets. They usually weigh from eighteen to twenty-eight pounds. They have the head of fair length, with square muzzle, the ears long and set low, the legs short or of medium length, and the coat fine and silky, wavy but not curly. Various colors are bred, as black, liver, red, black and white, black and tan, etc.

cockerel.c: Cockerel Cock"er*el (?), n. [Prob. a double dim. of cock.] A young cock.

cocket.c: Cocket Cock"et (?), a. [F. coquet coquettish. See Coquette, n.] Pert; saucy. [Obs.] Halliwell.
Cocket Cock"et, n. 1. (Eng. Law) A customhouse seal; a certified document given to a shipper as a warrant that his goods have been duly entered and have paid duty.

cockeye.c: Cockeye Cock"eye` (?), n. [From cock to turn up.] A squinting eye. Forby.
Cockeye Cock"eye`, n. (Mach.) The socket in the ball of a millstone, which sits on the cockhead.

cockfight.c: Cockfight Cock"fight` (?), n. A match or contest of gamecocks.

cockfighting.c: Cockfighting Cock"fight`ing, n. The act or practice of pitting gamecocks to fight.

cockhead.c: Cockhead Cock"head` (?), n. (Mach.) The rounded or pointed top of a grinding mill spindle, forming a pivot on which the stone is balanced.

cockhorse.c: Cockhorse Cock"horse`, a. 1. Lifted up, as one is on a tall horse.

cockle.c: Cockle Coc"kle (kŏk"k'l), n. [OE. cockes cockles, AS. sǣcoccas sea cockles, prob, from Celtic; cf. W. cocs cockles, Gael. cochull husk. Perh. influenced by F. coquille shell, a dim. from the root of E. conch. Cf. Coach.] 1. (Zool.) A bivalve mollusk, with radiating ribs, of the genus Cardium, especially Cardium edule, used in Europe for food; -- sometimes applied to similar shells of other genera.
Cockle Coc"kle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cockled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cockling (?).] [Of uncertian origin.] To cause to contract into wrinkles or ridges, as some kinds of cloth after a wetting.
Cockle Coc"kle, n. [AS. coccel, cocel; cf. Gael. cogall tares, husks, cockle.] (Bot.) (a) A plant or weed that grows among grain; the corn rose (Luchnis Githage). (b) The Lotium, or darnel.

cocklebur.c: Cocklebur Coc"kle*bur` (?), n. (Bot.) A coarse, composite weed, having a rough or prickly fruit; one of several species of the genus Xanthium; -- called also clotbur.

cockled.c: Cockled Coc"kled (?), a. Inclosed in a shell.

cockler.c: Cockler Coc"kler (?), n. One who takes and sells cockles.

cockleshell.c: Cockleshell Coc"kle*shell` (?), n. 1. One of the shells or valves of a cockle.

cockloft.c: Cockloft Cock"loft` (?; 115) n. [Prop., a loft where cocks roost.] An upper loft; a garret; the highest room in a building. Dryden. Swift.

cockmaster.c: Cockmaster Cock"mas`ter (?), n. One who breeds gamecocks. L'Estrange.

cockney.c: Cockney Cock"ney (kŏk"ny̆), n.; pl. Cockneys (-nĭz). [OE. cocknay, cokenay, a spoiled child, effeminate person, an egg; prob. orig. a cock's egg, a small imperfect egg; OE. cok cock + nay, neye, for ey egg (cf. Newt), AS. æg. See 1st Cock, Egg, n.] 1. An effeminate person; a spoilt child. “A young heir or cockney, that is his mother's darling.” Nash (1592).
Cockney Cock"ney, a. Of or relating to, or like, cockneys.

cockneydom.c: Cockneydom Cock"ney*dom (kŏk"nĭ*dŭm), n. The region or home of cockneys; cockneys, collectively. Thackeray.

cockneyfy.c: Cockneyfy Cock"ney*fy (-fī), v. t. [Cockney + -fy.] To form with the manners or character of a cockney. [Colloq.]

cockneyish.c: Cockneyish Cock"ney*ish, a. Characteristic of, or resembling, cockneys.

cockneyism.c: Cockneyism Cock"ney*ism (kŏk"nĭ*ĭz'm), n. The characteristics, manners, or dialect, of a cockney.

cockpit.c: Cockpit Cock"pit` (kŏk"pĭt), n. 1. A pit, or inclosed area, for cockfights.

cockroach.c: Cockroach Cock"roach (?), n. [Sp. cucaracha.] (Zool.) An orthopterous insect of the genus Blatta, and allied genera.

cockscomb.c: Cockscomb Cocks"comb` (kŏks"kōm`), n. [1st cock, n. + comb crest.] 1. See Coxcomb.

cockshead.c: Cockshead Cocks"head` (?), n. (Bot.) A leguminous herb (Onobrychis Caput-galli), having small spiny-crested pods.

cockshut.c: Cockshut Cock"shut` (?), n. A kind of net to catch woodcock. [Obs.] Nares.

cockshy.c: Cockshy Cock"shy` (?), n. 1. A game in which trinkets are set upon sticks, to be thrown at by the players; -- so called from an ancient popular sport which consisted in “shying” or throwing cudgels at live cocks.

cockspur.c: Cockspur Cock"spur (?), n. (Bot.) A variety of Cratægus, or hawthorn (Cratægus Crus-galli), having long, straight thorns; -- called also Cockspur thorn.

cockswain.c: Cockswain Cock"swain (?, colloq.?), n. [Cock a boat + swain; hence, the master of a boat.] The steersman of a boat; a petty officer who has charge of a boat and its crew.

cocktail.c: Cocktail Cock"tail` (?), n. 1. A beverage made of brandy, whisky, or gin, iced, flavored, and sweetened. [U. S.]

cockup.c: Cockup Cock"up (?), n. (Zool.) A large, highly esteemed, edible fish of India (Lates calcarifer); -- also called begti.

cockyoly.c: Cockyoly bird Cockyolly { Cock`y*ol"ly, or Cock`y*ol"y, bird } (?). [Cf. Cock, fowl; Yellow.] A pet name for any small bird.

coco.c: Coco palm Coco { Co"co (kō"ko), n. or Co"co palm (kō"ko päm`).} See Cocoa.

cocoa.c: Cocoa palm Cocoa { Co"coa (kō"ko), n., Co"coa palm` (kō"ko päm`) } [Sp. & Pg. coco cocoanut, in Sp. also, cocoa palm. The Portuguese name is said to have been given from the monkeylike face at the base of the nut, fr. Pg. coco a bugbear, an ugly mask to frighten children. Cf., however, Gr. koy^ki the cocoa palm and its fruit, ko`i:x, ko`i:kos, a kind of Egyptian palm.] (Bot.) A tall palm tree producing the cocoanut (Cocos nucifera) as its fruit. It grows in nearly all tropical countries, attaining a height of sixty or eighty feet. The trunk is without branches, and has a tuft of leaves at the top, each being fifteen or twenty feet in length, and at the base of these the nuts hang in clusters; the cocoanut tree. It is widely planted throughout the tropics, and in some locations as an ornamental tree.
Cocoa Co"coa, n. [Corrupted fr. cacao.] A preparation made from the seeds of the chocolate tree, and used in making, a beverage; also the beverage made from cocoa or cocoa shells.

cocobolas.c: Cocobolas Cocobolo { ‖Co`co*bo"lo (?), Co`co*bo"las (?) }, n. [Sp. cocobolo.] (Bot.) A very beautiful and hard wood, obtained in the West India Islands. It is used in cabinetmaking, for the handles of tools, and for various fancy articles.

cocoon.c: Cocoon Co*coon" (?), n. [F. cocon, dim. of coque shell of egge and insects, fr. L. concha mussel shell. See Conch.] 1. An oblong case in which the silkworm lies in its chrysalis state. It is formed of threads of silk spun by the worm just before leaving the larval state. From these the silk of commerce is prepared.

cocoonery.c: Cocoonery Co*coon"er*y (?), n. A building or apartment for silkworms, when feeding and forming cocoons.

coctible.c: Coctible Coc"ti*ble (?), a. [See Coctile.] Capable of being cooked. Blount.

coctile.c: Coctile Coc"tile (?), a. [L. coctilis, fr. coguere. See Cook.] Made by baking, or exposing to heat, as a brick.

coction.c: Coction Coc"tion (?), n. [L. coctio.] 1. Act of boiling.

cocus.c: cocus wood cocuswood co"cus*wood`, co"cus wood` (?). A West Indian wood obtained from the granadilla tree, used for making flutes, clarinets, and other musical instruments. [Also spelled cocoswood.]

cod.c: Cod Cod (kŏd), n. [AS. codd small bag; akin to Icel. koddi pillow, Sw. kudde cushion; cf. W. cod, cwd, bag, shell.]

Cod Cod, n. [Cf. G. gadde, and (in Heligoland) gadden, L. gadus merlangus.] (Zool.) An important edible fish (Gadus morrhua), taken in immense numbers on the northern coasts of Europe and America. It is especially abundant and large on the Grand Bank of Newfoundland. It is salted and dried in large quantities.
Cod liver Cod" liv`er (?), n. The liver of the common cod and allied species.

coda.c: Coda ‖Co"da (kō"dȧ), n. [It., tail, fr. L. cauda.] (Mus.) A few measures added beyond the natural termination of a composition.

codder.c: Codder Cod"der (?), n. A gatherer of cods or peas. [Obs. or Prov.] Johnson.

coddle.c: Coddle Cod"dle (kŏd"d'l), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coddled (-d'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Coddling (-dlĭng).] [Cf. Prov. E. caddle to coax, spoil, fondle, and Cade, a. & v. t.] [Written also codle.] 1. To parboil, or soften by boiling.

coddymoddy.c: Coddymoddy Cod"dy*mod"dy (kŏd"dy̆*mŏd"dy̆), n. (Zool.) A gull in the plumage of its first year.

code.c: Code Code (kōd), n. [F., fr. L. codex, caudex, the stock or stem of a tree, a board or tablet of wood smeared over with wax, on which the ancients originally wrote; hence, a book, a writing.] 1. A body of law, sanctioned by legislation, in which the rules of law to be specifically applied by the courts are set forth in systematic form; a compilation of laws by public authority; a digest.

codefendant.c: Codefendant Co`de*fend"ant (?), n. A joint defendant. Blackstone.

codeine.c: Codeine Co"deine (kō"dēn or ko*dē"ĭn), n. [Gr. kw`deia poppy head: cf. F. codéine.] (Chem.) One of the opium alkaloids; a white crystalline substance, C18H21NO3, similar to and regarded as a derivative of morphine, but much feebler in its action; -- called also codeia.

codetta.c: Codetta ‖Co*det"ta (ko*dĕt"tȧ), n. [It., dim. of coda tail.] (Mus.) A short passage connecting two sections, but not forming part of either; a short coda.

codex.c: Codex ‖Co"dex (kō"dĕks), n.; pl. Codices (#). [L. See Code.] 1. A book, especially an early form of book with pages stitched together, contrasting with the earlier scrolls; a manuscript; as, a DaVinci codex.

codfish.c: Codfish Cod"fish (?), n. (Zool.) A kind of fish. Same as Cod.

codger.c: Codger Codg"er (?), n. [Cf. Cadger.] 1. A miser or mean person.

codical.c: Codical Cod"i*cal (?), a. Relating to a codex, or a code.

codicil.c: Codicil Cod"i*cil (?), n. [L. codicillus, dim. of codex: cf. F. codicille. See Code.] (Law) A clause added to a will.

codicillary.c: Codicillary Cod`i*cil"la*ry (?), a. [L. codicillaris, codicillarius.] Of the nature of a codicil.

codification.c: Codification Co`di*fi*ca"tion (? or?), n. [Cf. F. codification.] The act or process of codifying or reducing laws to a code.

codifier.c: Codifier Co"di*fi`er (? or?), n. One who codifies.

codify.c: Codify Co"di*fy (? or?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Codified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Codifying.] [Code + -fy: cf. F. codifier.] To reduce to a code, as laws.

codilla.c: Codilla Co*dil"la (?), n. [Cf. L. codicula a little tail, dim. of cauda tail.] (Com.) The coarse tow of flax and hemp. McElrath.

codille.c: Codille Co*dille" (?), n. [F. codile.] A term at omber, signifying that the game is won. Pope.

codist.c: Codist Co"dist (?), n. A codifier; a maker of codes. [R.]

codling.c: Codling Codlin { Cod"lin (?), Cod"ling (?) }, n. [Cf. AS. codæppel a quince.] (a) An apple fit to stew or coddle. (b) An immature apple.
Codling Cod"ling, n. [Dim. of cod the fish.] (Zool.) A young cod; also, a hake.

codpiece.c: Codpiece Cod"piece` (?), n. [Cod, n.,? + piece.] A part of male dress in front of the breeches, formerly made very conspicuous. Shak. Fosbroke.

coefficiency.c: Coefficiency Co`ef*fi"cien*cy (?), n. Joint efficiency; cooperation. Glanvill.

coefficient.c: Coefficient Co`ef*fi"cient (?), a. Cooperating; acting together to produce an effect.
Coefficient Co`ef*fi"cient, n. 1. That which unites in action with something else to produce the same effect.

coehorn.c: Coehorn Coe"horn (?), n. [From its inventor, Baron Coehorn.] (Mil.) A small bronze mortar mounted on a wooden block with handles, and light enough to be carried short distances by two men.

coelacanth.c: Coelacanth Cœl"a*canth (? or?), a. [Gr. koi^los hollow +? spine.] (Zool.) Having hollow spines, as some ganoid fishes.

coelenterata.c: Coelenterata Coelentera { ‖Cœ*len"te*ra (?) or ‖Cœ*len`te*ra"ta, } n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. koi^los hollow +? intestines.] (Zool.) A comprehensive group of Invertebrata, mostly marine, comprising the Anthozoa, Hydrozoa, and Ctenophora. The name implies that the stomach and body cavities are one. The group is sometimes enlarged so as to include the sponges.

coelenterate.c: Coelenterate Cœ*len"ter*ate (?), a. (Zool.) Belonging to the Cœlentera. -- n. One of the Cœlentera.

coelia.c: Coelia ‖Cœ"li*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. koili`a a cavity of the body, a ventricle.] (Anat.) A cavity.

coelodont.c: Coelodont Cœ"lo*dont (?), a. [Gr. koi^los hollow +?,?, tooth.] (Zool.) Having hollow teeth; -- said of a group lizards. -- n. One of a group of lizards having hollow teeth.

coelospermous.c: Coelospermous Cœl`o*sper"mous (? or?), a. [Gr. koi^los hollow +? seed.] (Bot.) Hollow-seeded; having the ventral face of the seedlike carpels incurved at the ends, as in coriander seed.

coelum.c: Coelum ‖Cœ"lum (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a hollow, neut. of koi^los hollow.] (Anat.) See Body cavity, under Body.

coemption.c: Coemption Co*emp"tion (?; 215), n. [L. coëmptio, fr. coëmere to buy up. See Emption.] The act of buying the whole quantity of any commodity. [R.] Bacon.

coendoo.c: Coendoo ‖Co*en"doo (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) The Brazilian porcupine (Cercolades prehensiles syn. Sphingurus prehensiles), remarkable for its prehensile tail.

coenenchyma.c: Coenenchyma Coenenchym { Cœ*nen"chym (?), ‖Cœ*nen"chy*ma (?) } n. [NL. coenenchyma, fr. Gr. koino`s common +? something poured in. Formed like parenchyma.] (Zool.) The common tissue which unites the polyps or zooids of a compound anthozoan or coral. It may be soft or more or less ossified. See Coral.

coenesthesis.c: Coenesthesis ‖Cœn`es*the"sis (? or?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. koino`s common +? sensation.] (Physiol.) Common sensation or general sensibility, as distinguished from the special sensations which are located in, or ascribed to, separate organs, as the eye and ear. It is supposed to depend on the ganglionic system.

coenobite.c: Coenobite coenobite coenobite, Cœn"o*bite (? or?), n. a member of a religious order living in common. Same as Cenobite.

coenoecium.c: Coenoecium ‖Cœ*nœ"ci*um (? or?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. koino`s common + o'i^kos house.] (Zool.) The common tissue which unites the various zooids of a bryozoan.

coenogamy.c: Coenogamy Cœ*nog"a*my (?), n. [Gr.?; koino`s common +? marraige.] The state of a community which permits promiscuous sexual intercourse among its members; -- as in certain primitive tribes or communistic societies. [Written also cenogamy.]

coenosarc.c: Coenosarc Cœn"o*sarc (? or?), n. [Gr. koino`s common +?,?, flesh.] (Zool.) The common soft tissue which unites the polyps of a compound hydroid. See Hydroidea.

coenurus.c: Coenurus ‖Cœ*nu"rus (?), n. [NL. fr. Gr. koino`s common + o'yra` tail.] (Zool.) The larval stage of a tapeworm (Tænia cœnurus) which forms bladderlike sacs in the brain of sheep, causing the fatal disease known as water brain, vertigo, staggers or gid.

coequal.c: Coequal Co*e"qual (?), a. [L. coaequalis; co- + aequalis equal.] Being on an equality in rank or power. -- n. One who is on an equality with another.

coequality.c: Coequality Co`e*qual"i*ty (?), n. The state of being on an equality, as in rank or power.

coerce.c: Coerce Co*erce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coerced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coercing.] [L. coërcere; co- + arcere to shut up, to press together. See Ark.] 1. To restrain by force, especially by law or authority; to repress; to curb. Burke.

coercible.c: Coercible Co"er"ci*ble (?), a. Capable of being coerced.

coercion.c: Coercion Co*er"cion (?), n. [L. coercio, fr. coercere. See Coerce.] 1. The act or process of coercing.

coercitive.c: Coercitive Co*er"ci*tive (?), a. Coercive. “Coercitive power in laws.” Jer. Taylor.

coercive.c: Coercive Co*er"cive (?), a. Serving or intended to coerce; having power to constrain.

coerulignone.c: Coerulignone Cœ`ru*lig"none (?), n. [L. coeruleus cerulean + lignum wood + E. quinone.] (Chem.) A bluish violet, crystalline substance obtained in the purification of crude wood vinegar. It is regarded as a complex quinone derivative of diphenyl; -- called also cedriret.

coessential.c: Coessential Co`es*sen"tial (?), a. Partaking of the same essence. -- Co`es*sen"tial*ly, adv.

coessentiality.c: Coessentiality Co`es*sen`ti*al"i*ty (? or?; 106), n. Participation of the same essence. Johnson.

coestablishment.c: Coestablishment Co`es*tab"lish*ment (?), n. Joint establishment. Bp. Watson.

coetanean.c: Coetanean Co`e*ta"ne*an (?), n. A person coetaneous with another; a contemporary. [R.]

coetaneous.c: Coetaneous Co`e*ta"ne*ous (?), a. [L. coaetaneus; co- + aetas age.] Of the same age; beginning to exist at the same time; contemporaneous.

coeternal.c: Coeternal Co`e*ter"nal (?), a. Equally eternal. -- Co`e*ter"nal*ly, adv.

coeternity.c: Coeternity Co`e*ter"ni*ty (?), n. Existence from eternity equally with another eternal being; equal eternity.

coeval.c: Coeval Co*e"val (?), a. [L. coaevus; co- + aevum lifetime, age. See Age, n.] Of the same age; existing during the same period of time, especially time long and remote; -- usually followed by with.
Coeval Co*e"val, n. One of the same age; a contemporary.

coexist.c: Coexist Co`ex*ist (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Coexisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Coexisting.] To exist at the same time; -- sometimes followed by with.

coexistence.c: Coexistence Co`ex*ist"ence (?), n. Existence at the same time with another; -- contemporary existence.

coexistent.c: Coexistent Co`ex*ist"ent (?), a. Existing at the same time with another. -- n. That which coexists with another.

coextend.c: Coextend Co`ex*tend, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coextended; p. pr. & vb. n. Coextending.] To extend through the same space or time with another; to extend to the same degree.

coextension.c: Coextension Co`ex*ten"sion (kō`ĕks*tĕn"shŭn), n. The act of extending equally, or the state of being equally extended.

coextensive.c: Coextensive Co`ex*ten"sive (?), a. Equally extensive; having equal extent; as, consciousness and knowledge are coextensive. Sir W. Hamilton. -- Co`ex*ten"sive*ly, adv. -- Co`ex*ten"sive*ness, n.

coffee.c: Coffee Cof"fee (kä"fe; kŏf"fe; 115), n. [Turk. qahveh, Ar. qahuah wine, coffee, a decoction of berries. Cf. Café.] 1. The “beans” or “berries” (pyrenes) obtained from the drupes of a small evergreen tree of the genus Coffea, growing in Abyssinia, Arabia, Persia, and other warm regions of Asia and Africa, and also in tropical America.

coffeehouse.c: Coffeehouse Cof"fee*house` (kä"fe*hous`), n. A house of entertainment, where guests are supplied with coffee and other refreshments, and where men meet for conversation.

coffeeman.c: Coffeeman Cof"fee*man (?), n. One who keeps a coffeehouse. Addison.

coffeepot.c: coffeepot coffee-pot cof"fee-pot, cof"fee*pot (?), n. 1. A covered pot in which coffee is prepared, or is brought upon the table for drinking.

coffeeroom.c: Coffeeroom Cof"fee*room` (?), n. A public room where coffee and other refreshments may be obtained.

coffer.c: Coffer Cof"fer (?; 115), n. [OF. cofre, F. coffre, L. cophinus basket, fr. Gr.?. Cf. Coffin, n.] 1. A casket, chest, or trunk; especially, one used for keeping money or other valuables. Chaucer.
Coffer Cof"fer, v. t. 1. To put into a coffer. Bacon.

cofferdam.c: Cofferdam Cof"fer*dam (?), n. A water-tight inclosure, as of piles packed with clay, from which the water is pumped to expose the bottom (of a river, etc.) and permit the laying of foundations, building of piers, etc.

cofferer.c: Cofferer Cof"fer*er (?), n. One who keeps treasures in a coffer. [R.]

cofferwork.c: Cofferwork Cof"fer*work` (?), n. (Masonry) Rubblework faced with stone. Knight.

coffin.c: Coffin Cof"fin (?; 115), n. [OE., a basket, receptacle, OF. cofin, fr. L. cophinus. See Coffer, n.] 1. The case in which a dead human body is inclosed for burial.
Coffin Cof"fin, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coffined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Coffining.] To inclose in, or as in, a coffin.

coffle.c: Coffle Cof"fle (?; 115), n. [Ar. kafala caravan.] A gang of negro slaves being driven to market.

cog.c: Cog Cog (kŏg), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cogged (kŏgd); p. pr. & vb. n. Cogging.] [Cf. W. coegio to make void, to beceive, from coeg empty, vain, foolish. Cf. Coax, v. t.]
Cog Cog (?), v. i. To deceive; to cheat; to play false; to lie; to wheedle; to cajole.
Cog Cog, n. A trick or deception; a falsehood. Wm. Watson.

Cog Cog, n. [Cf. Sw. kugge a cog, or W. cocos the cogs of a wheel.] 1. (Mech.) A tooth, cam, or catch for imparting or receiving motion, as on a gear wheel, or a lifter or wiper on a shaft; originally, a separate piece of wood set in a mortise in the face of a wheel.
Cog Cog, v. t. To furnish with a cog or cogs.
Cog Cog, n. [OE. cogge; cf. D. kog, Icel. kuggr Cf. Cock a boat.] A small fishing boat. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

cogency.c: Cogency Co"gen*cy (?), n. [See Cogent.] The quality of being cogent; power of compelling conviction; conclusiveness; force.

cogent.c: Cogent Co"gent (?), a. [L. cogens, p. pr. of cogere to drive together, to force; co- + agere to drive. See Agent, a., and cf. Coact to force, Coagulate, p. a.] 1. Compelling, in a physical sense; powerful. [Obs.]

cogently.c: Cogently Co"gent*ly, adv. In a cogent manner; forcibly; convincingly; conclusively. Locke.

cogger.c: Cogger Cog"ger (?), n. [From Cog to wheedle.] A flatterer or deceiver; a sharper.

coggery.c: Coggery Cog"ger*y, n. Trick; deception. Bp. Watson.

coggle.c: Coggle Cog"gle (?), n. [See Cog small boat.] A small fishing boat. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
Coggle Cog"gle, n. [Cf. Cobble a cobblestone.] A cobblestone. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

cogitability.c: Cogitability Cog`i*ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being cogitable; conceivableness.

cogitable.c: Cogitable Cog"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. cogitabilis, fr. cogitare to think.] Capable of being brought before the mind as a thought or idea; conceivable; thinkable.

cogitabund.c: Cogitabund Cog"i*ta*bund` (?), a. [L. cogitabundus.] Full of thought; thoughtful. [R.] Leigh Hunt.

cogitate.c: Cogitate Cog"i*tate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Cogitated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Cogitating.] [L. cogitatus, p. p. of cogitare to reflect upon, prob. fr. co- + the root of aio I say; hence, prop., to discuss with one's self. Cf. Adage.] To engage in continuous thought; to think.
Cogitate Cog"i*tate, v. t. To think over; to plan.

cogitation.c: Cogitation Cog`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. cogitatio: cf. F. cogitation.] The act of thinking; thought; meditation; contemplation. “Fixed in cogitation deep.” Milton.

cogitative.c: Cogitative Cog"i*ta*tive (?), a. [Cf. LL. cogitativus.] 1. Possessing, or pertaining to, the power of thinking or meditating. “Cogitative faculties.” Wollaston.

cogman.c: Cogman Cog"man (?), n. A dealer in cogware or coarse cloth. [Obs.] Wright.

cognac.c: Cognac Co"gnac` (?), n. [F.] A kind of French brandy, so called from the town of Cognac.

cognate.c: Cognate Cog"nate (?), a. [L. cognatus; co- + gnatus, natus, p. p. of nasci, anciently gnasci, to be born. See Nation, and cf. Connate.] 1. Allied by blood; kindred by birth; specifically (Law), related on the mother's side.
Cognate Cog"nate, n. 1. (Law) One who is related to another on the female side. Wharton.

cognateness.c: Cognateness Cog"nate*ness, n. The state of being cognate.

cognati.c: Cognati ‖Cog*na"ti (?), n. pl. [L.] (Law) Relatives by the mother's side. Wharton.

cognation.c: Cognation Cog*na"tion (?), n. [L. cognatio.] 1. Relationship by blood; descent from the same original; kindred.

cognatus.c: Cognatus ‖Cog*na"tus (?), n. [L., a kinsman.] (Law) A person connected through cognation.

cognisee.c: Cognisee Cognisor { Cog`ni*sor" (? or?), Cog`ni*see (?), } n. See Cognizor, Cognizee.

cognition.c: Cognition Cog*ni"tion (?), n. [L. cognitio, fr. cognoscere, cognitum, to become acquainted with, to know; co- + noscere, gnoscere, to get a knowledge of. See Know, v. t.] 1. The act of knowing; knowledge; perception.

cognitive.c: Cognitive Cog"ni*tive (?), a. Knowing, or apprehending by the understanding; as, cognitive power. South.

cognizable.c: Cognizable Cog"ni*za*ble (? or?), a. [F. connaissable, fr. connaître to know, L. cognoscere. See Cognition.] 1. Capable of being known or apprehended; as, cognizable causes.

cognizably.c: Cognizably Cog"ni*za*bly, adv. In a cognizable manner.

cognizance.c: Cognizance Cog"ni*zance (? or?; 277), n. [OF. conissance, conoissance, F. connaissance, LL. cognoscentia, fr. L. cognoscere to know. See Cognition, and cf. Cognoscence, Connoisseur.] 1. Apprehension by the understanding; perception; observation.

cognizant.c: Cognizant Cog"ni*zant (? or?), a. [See Cognizance, and cf. Connusant.] Having cognizance or knowledge. (of).

cognize.c: Cognize Cog"nize (?), v. t. [Cf. Cognizant, Recognize.] To know or perceive; to recognize.

cognizee.c: Cognizee Cog`ni*zee" (? or?), n. (Law) One to whom a fine of land was acknowledged. Blackstone.
