cotta.c: Cotta Cot"ta (?), n. [LL. See Coat.] 1. (Eccl.) A surplice, in England and America usually one shorter and less full than the ordinary surplice and with short sleeves, or sometimes none.

cottage.c: Cottage Cot"tage (k?t"t?j; 48), n. [From Cot a cottage.] A small house; a cot; a hut.

cottaged.c: Cottaged Cot"taged (-t?jd), a. Set or covered with cottages.

cottagely.c: Cottagely Cot"tage*ly (-t?j-l?), a. Cottagelike; suitable for a cottage; rustic. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

cottager.c: Cottager Cot"ta*ger (k?t"t?-j?r), n. 1. One who lives in a cottage.

cottar.c: Cottar Cotter { Cot"ter, Cot"tar } (k?t"t?r), n. [LL. cotarius, cottarius, coterius. See Cot.] A cottager; a cottier. Burns.

cotter.c: Cotter Cot"ter (kŏt"tẽr), n. 1. A piece of wood or metal, commonly wedge-shaped, used for fastening together parts of a machine or structure. It is driven into an opening through one or all of the parts. In the United States a cotter is commonly called a key.
Cotter Cot"ter, v. t. To fasten with a cotter.

cottier.c: Cottier Cot"ti*er (-tĭ*ẽr), n. [OF. cotier. See Coterie, and cf. Cotter.] In Great Britain and Ireland, a person who hires a small cottage, with or without a plot of land. Cottiers commonly aid in the work of the landlord's farm. [Written also cottar and cotter.]

cottise.c: Cottise Cot"tise (kŏt"tĭs), n. [Cf. F. côté side, L. costa rib.] (Her.) A diminutive of the bendlet, containing one half its area or one quarter the area of the bend. When a single cottise is used alone it is often called a cost. See also Couple-close.

cottised.c: Cottised Cot"tised (-t?st), a. (Her.) Set between two cottises, -- said of a bend; or between two barrulets, -- said of a bar or fess.

cottoid.c: Cottoid Cot"toid (k?t"toid), a. [NL. cottus sculpin + -oid.] (Zool.) Like a fish of the genus Cottus. -- n. A fish belonging to, or resembling, the genus Cottus. See Sculpin.

cottolene.c: Cottolene Cot"to*lene` (kŏt"to*lēn`), n. A product from cotton-seed, used as lard.

cotton.c: Cotton Cot"ton (kŏt"t'n), n. [F. coton, Sp. algodon the cotton plant and its wool, coton printed cotton, cloth, fr. Ar. qutun, alqutun, cotton wool. Cf. Acton, Hacqueton.] 1. A soft, downy substance, resembling fine wool, consisting of the unicellular twisted hairs which grow on the seeds of the cotton plant. Long-staple cotton has a fiber sometimes almost two inches long; short-staple, from two thirds of an inch to an inch and a half.
Cotton Cot"ton, v. i. 1. To rise with a regular nap, as cloth does. [Obs.]
Cotton batting Cot"ton bat"ting. Cotton prepared in sheets or rolls for quilting, upholstering, and similar purposes.
Cotton State Cotton State. Alabama; -- a nickname.

cottonade.c: Cottonade Cot"ton*ade` (k?t"t'n-?d`), n. [F. cottonade.] A somewhat stout and thick fabric of cotton.

cottonary.c: Cottonary Cot"ton*a*ry (-?-r?), a. Relating to, or composed of, cotton; cottony. [Obs.]

cottonseed.c: cottonseed cotton seed { cotton seed, or, usually collectively, cot"ton*seed` } (?), n. The seed of the cotton plant.
Cottonseed meal Cottonseed meal. A meal made from hulled cotton seeds after the oil has been expressed.

Cottonseed oil Cottonseed oil. A fixed, semidrying oil extracted from cottonseed. It is pale yellow when pure (sp. gr.,.92-.93). and is extensively used in soap making, in cookery, and as an adulterant of other oils.

cottontail.c: Cottontail Cot"ton*tail` (kŏt"t'n*tāl`), n. (Zool.) The American wood rabbit (Lepus sylvaticus); -- also called Molly cottontail.

cottonwood.c: Cottonwood Cot"ton*wood` (-wŏod`), n. (Bot.) An American tree of the genus Populus or poplar, having the seeds covered with abundant cottonlike hairs; esp., the Populus monilifera and Populus angustifolia of the Western United States.

cottony.c: Cottony Cot"ton*y (-?), a. 1. Covered with hairs or pubescence, like cotton; downy; nappy; woolly.

cottrel.c: Cottrel Cot"trel (k?t"tr?l), n. A trammel, or hook to support a pot over a fire. Knight.

cotyle.c: Cotyle Cotyla { Cot"y*la (k?t"?-l?), Cot"y*le (k?t"?-l?), } n. [Gr.??? anything hollow, cup of a joint, small meassure: cf. L. cotyla a measure.] (Anat.) A cuplike cavity or organ. Same as Acetabulum.

cotyledon.c: Cotyledon Cot`y*le"don (k?t`?-l?"d?n), n. [Gr.??? a cupshaped hollow, fr.???. See Cotyle.] 1. (Anat.) One of the patches of villi found in some forms of placenta.

cotyledonal.c: Cotyledonal Cot`y*led"on*al (k?t`?-l?d"?n-ail), a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a cotyledon.

cotyledonary.c: Cotyledonary Cot`y*led"on*a*ry (-?-r?), a. Having a cotyledon; tufted; as, the cotyledonary placenta of the cow.

cotyledonous.c: Cotyledonous Cot`y*led"on*ous (-?s; 277), a. Of or pertaining to a cotyledon or cotyledons; having a seed lobe.

cotyliform.c: Cotyliform Co*tyl"i*form (k?-t?l"?-f?rm), a. [Cotyle + -form.] (Zool.) Shaped like a cotyle or a cup.

cotyloidal.c: cotyloidal cotyloid cot"y*loid, cotyloidal (k?t"?-loid), a. [Cotyle + -oid] (Anat.) (a) Shaped like a cup; cup-shaped; as, the cotyloid cavity, the cup-shaped socket which receives the head of the thigh bone. (b) Pertaining to a cotyloid cavity; as, the cotyloid ligament, or notch.

coucal.c: Coucal ‖Cou"cal (k??"k?l), n. [Prob. native name.] (Zool.) A large, Old World, ground cuckoo of the genus Centropus, of several species.

couch.c: Couch Couch (kouch), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Couched (koucht); p. pr. & vb. n. Couching.] [F. coucher to lay down, lie down, OF. colchier, fr. L. collocare to lay, put, place; col- + locare to place, fr. locus place. See Locus.]
Couch Couch, v. i. 1. To lie down or recline, as on a bed or other place of rest; to repose; to lie.
Couch Couch, n. [F. couche, OF. colche, culche, fr. colchier. See Couch, v. t. ] 1. A bed or place for repose or sleep; particularly, in the United States, a lounge.
Couch grass Couch" grass` (gr?s`). (Bot.) See Quitch grass.

couchancy.c: Couchancy Couch"an*cy (kouch"an-s?), n. State of lying down for repose. [R.]

couchant.c: Couchant Couch"ant (kouch"ant), a. [F., p. pr. of coucher. See Couch, v. t.] 1. Lying down with head erect; squatting.

couche.c: Couche ‖Cou`ché" (k??`sh?"), a. [F., p. p. of coucher. See Couch, v. t. ] (Her.) (a) Not erect; inclined; -- said of anything that is usually erect, as an escutcheon. (b) Lying on its side; thus, a chevron couché is one which emerges from one side of the escutcheon and has its apex on the opposite side, or at the fess point.

couchee.c: Couchee Cou"chee (k??"sh?; F. k??"sh?"), n. [F. couch?e a sleeping place from coucher. See Couch, v. t. ] A reception held at the time of going to bed, as by a sovereign or great prince. [Obs.] Dryden. The duke's levees and couchees were so crowded that the antechambers were full. Bp. Burnet.

couching.c: Couching Couch"ing, n. 1. (Med.) The operation of putting down or displacing the opaque lens in cataract.

couchless.c: Couchless Couch"less (kouch"l?s), a. Having no couch or bed.

coudee.c: Coudee Cou"dee (k??"d?; F. k??`d?"), n. [F. coud?e, from coude elbow.] A measure of length; the distance from the elbow to the end of the middle finger; a cubit.

cougar.c: Cougar Cou"gar (k??"g?r), n. [F. couguar, from the native name in the South American dialects, cuguacuara, cuguacuarana.] (Zool.) An American feline quadruped (Felis concolor), resembling the African panther in size and habits. Its color is tawny, without spots; hence writers often called it the American lion. Called also puma, panther, mountain lion, and catamount. See Puma.

cough.c: Cough Cough (k?f), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Coughed (k?ft); p. pr. & vb. n. Coughing.] [Cf. D. kuchen, MHG. k?chen to breathe, G. keuchen to pant, and E. chincough, the first part of which is prob. akin to cough; cf. also E. choke.] To expel air, or obstructing or irritating matter, from the lungs or air passages, in a noisy and violent manner.
Cough Cough, v. t. 1. To expel from the lungs or air passages by coughing; -- followed by up; as, to cough up phlegm.

Cough Cough, n. [Cg. D. kuch. See Cough, v. i. ] 1. A sudden, noisy, and violent expulsion of air from the chest, caused by irritation in the air passages, or by the reflex action of nervous or gastric disorder, etc.

could.c: Could Could (k??d), imp. of Can. [OF. coude. The l was inserted by mistake, under the influence of should and would.] Was, should be, or would be, able, capable, or susceptible. Used as an auxiliary, in the past tense or in the conditional present.

coulee.c: Coulee ‖Cou`lee" (k??`l?"), n. [F. coulée, fr. couler to run or flow.] A stream; (Geol.) a stream of lava. Also, in the Western United States, the bed of a stream, even if dry, when deep and having inclined sides; distinguished from a cañon, which has precipitous sides.

couleur.c: Couleur ‖Cou`leur" (?), n. [F.] 1. Color; -- chiefly used in a few French phrases, as couler de rose, color of rose; and hence, adjectively, rose-colored; roseate.

coulisse.c: Coulisse ‖Cou*lisse" (kŏo*lĭs"; F. kōo`les"), n. [F., fr. couler to flow, glide.] 1. A piece of timber having a groove in which something glides.
Coulisse Cou*lisse" (kōo*lēs"), n. 1. A fluting in a sword blade.

couloir.c: Couloir ‖Cou`loir" (k??`lw?r"), n. [F., a strainer.] 1. A deep gorge; a gully.

coulomb.c: Coulomb ‖Cou`lomb" (k??`l?n"), n. [From Coulomb, a French physicist and electrican.] (Physics) The standard unit of quantity in electrical measurements. It is the quantity of electricity conveyed in one second by the current produced by an electro-motive force of one volt acting in a circuit having a resistance of one ohm, or the quantity transferred by one ampère in one second. Formerly called weber.
Coulomb meter Cou`lomb" me"ter (?). (Elec.) Any instrument by which electricity can be measured in coulombs.

coulombs.c: Coulomb's law Cou`lomb's" law (?). (Physics) The law that the force exerted between two electric or magnetic charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely to the square of the distance between them.

coulure.c: Coulure Cou*lure" (?), n. [F., prop., a dropping.] (Hort.) A disease affecting grapes, esp. in California, manifested by the premature dropping of the fruit.

coumaric.c: Coumaric Cou*mar"ic (k??-m?r"?k), a. Relating to, derived from, or like, the Dipterix odorata, a tree of Guiana.

coumarin.c: Coumarin Cou"ma*rin (kōo"mȧ*rĭn), n. [F., fr. coumarou, a tree of Guiana.] (Chem.) The concrete essence of the tonka bean, the fruit of Dipterix (formerly Coumarouna) odorata and consisting essentially of coumarin proper, which is a white crystalline substance, C9H6O2, of vanilla-like odor, regarded as an anhydride of coumaric acid, and used in flavoring. Coumarin in also made artificially.

coumarou.c: Coumarou ‖Cou"ma*rou (?), n. [See Coumarin.] (Bot.) The tree (Dipteryx odorata) which bears the tonka bean; also, the bean itself.

council.c: Council Coun"cil (koun"sĭl), n. [F. concile, fr. L. concilium; con- + calare to call, akin to Gr.??? to call, and E. hale, v., haul. Cf. Conciliate. This word is often confounded with counsel, with which it has no connection.]

councilist.c: Councilist Coun"cil*ist (koun"s?l-?st), n. One who belongs to a council; one who gives an opinion. [Obs.]

councilman.c: Councilman Coun"cil*man (koun"sĭl*main), n.; pl. Councilmen (koun"sĭl*mein). A member of a council, especially of the common council of a city; a councilor.

councilor.c: Councilor Coun"cil*or (koun"s?l-?r), n. A member of a council. [Written also councillor.]

coune.c: Co-une Co`-une" (k?`?n"), v. t. [L. co- + unus one.] To combine or unite. [Obs.] “Co-uned together.” Feltham.

counite.c: Co-unite Co`-u*nite", a. United closely with another. [Obs.]

counsel.c: Counsel Coun"sel (koun"sĕl), n. [OE. conseil, F. conseil, fr. L. consilium, fr. the root of consulere to consult, of uncertain origin. Cf. Consult, Consul.] 1. Interchange of opinions; mutual advising; consultation.

Counsel Coun"sel, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counseled (-sĕld) or Counselled; p. pr. & vb. n. Counseling or Counselling.] [OE. conseilen, counseilen, F. conseiller, fr. L. consiliari, fr. consilium counsel.] 1. To give advice to; to advice, admonish, or instruct, as a person.

counselable.c: Counselable Coun"sel*a*ble (-ȧ*b'l), a. [Written also counsellable.] 1. Willing to receive counsel or follow advice. [R.]

counselor.c: Counselor Coun"sel*or (koun"sĕl*ẽr), n. [Written also counsellor.] [OE. conseiler, F. conseiller, fr. L. consiliarius, fr. consilium counsel.] 1. One who counsels; an adviser.

counselorship.c: Counselorship Coun"sel*or*ship (koun"s?l-?r-sh?p), n. The function and rank or office of a counselor. Bacon.

count.c: Count Count (kount), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counted; p. pr. & vb. n. Counting.] [OF. conter, and later (etymological spelling) compter, in modern French thus distinguished; conter to relate (cf. Recount, Account), compter to count; fr. L. computuare to reckon, compute; com- + putare to reckon, settle, order, prune, orig., to clean. See Pure, and cf. Compute.] 1. To tell or name one by one, or by groups, for the purpose of ascertaining the whole number of units in a collection; to number; to enumerate; to compute; to reckon.

Count Count, v. i. 1. To number or be counted; to possess value or carry weight; hence, to increase or add to the strength or influence of some party or interest; as, every vote counts; accidents count for nothing.

Count Count, n. [F. conte and compte, with different meanings, fr. L. computus a computation, fr. computare. See Count, v. t.] 1. The act of numbering; reckoning; also, the number ascertained by counting.

Count Count, n. [F. conte, fr. L. comes, comitis, associate, companion, one of the imperial court or train, properly, one who goes with another; com- + ire to go, akin to Skr. i to go.] A nobleman on the continent of Europe, equal in rank to an English earl.

countable.c: Countable Count"a*ble (-?-b'l), a. Capable of being numbered.

countenance.c: Countenance Coun"te*nance (koun"te*nains), n. [OE. contenance, countenaunce, demeanor, composure, F. contenance demeanor, fr. L. continentia continence, LL. also, demeanor, fr. L. continere to hold together, repress, contain. See Contain, and cf. Continence.] 1. Appearance or expression of the face; look; aspect; mien.
Countenance Coun"te*nance (koun"t?-nans), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countenanced (-nanst); p. pr. & vb. n. Countenancing.] 1. To encourage; to favor; to approve; to aid; to abet.

countenancer.c: Countenancer Coun"te*nan*cer (-nan-s?r), n. One who countenances, favors, or supports.

counter.c: Counter- Coun"ter- (koun"tẽr-). A prefix meaning contrary, opposite, in opposition; as, counteract, counterbalance, countercheck. See Counter, adv. & a.

Counter Count"er (koun"tẽr), n. [OE. countere, countour, a counter (in sense 1), OF. contere, conteor, fr. conter to count. See Count, v. t. ] 1. One who counts, or reckons up; a calculator; a reckoner.

Counter Coun"ter, n. [OE. countour, OF. contouer, comptouer, F. comptoir, LL. computatorium, prop., a computing place, place of accounts, fr. L. computare. See Count, v. t.] A table or board on which money is counted and over which business is transacted; a long, narrow table or bench, on which goods are laid for examination by purchasers, or on which they are weighed or measured.
Counter Coun"ter, adv. [F. contre, fr. L. contra against. Cf. Contra-.] 1. Contrary; in opposition; in an opposite direction; contrariwise; -- used chiefly with run or go.

Counter Coun"ter, a. Contrary; opposite; contrasted; opposed; adverse; antagonistic; as, a counter current; a counter revolution; a counter poison; a counter agent; counter fugue. “Innumerable facts attesting the counter principle.” I. Taylor.
Counter Coun"ter, n. [See Counter, adv., Contra.] 1. (Naut.) The after part of a vessel's body, from the water line to the stern, -- below and somewhat forward of the stern proper.
Counter Coun"ter, v. i. (Boxing) To return a blow while receiving one, as in boxing.
Counter brace Coun"ter brace` (br?s`). 1. (Naut.) The brace of the fore-topsail on the leeward side of a vessel.
Counter tenor Coun"ter ten`or (t?n`?r). [OF. contreteneur. Cf. Contratenor, and see Tenor a part in music.] (Mus.) One of the middle parts in music, between the tenor and the treble; high tenor.

counteract.c: Counteract Coun`ter*act" (koun`t?r-?kt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counteracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Counteracting.] To act in opposition to; to hinder, defeat, or frustrate, by contrary agency or influence; as, to counteract the effect of medicines; to counteract good advice.

counteraction.c: Counteraction Coun`ter*ac"tion (koun`t?r-?k"sh?n), n. Action in opposition; hindrance resistance.

counteractive.c: Counteractive Coun`ter*act"ive, n. One who, or that which, counteracts.

counterbalance.c: Counterbalance Coun`ter*bal"ance (-b?l"ans), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterbalanced (-anst); p. pr. & vb. n. Counterbalancing.] To oppose with an equal weight or power; to counteract the power or effect of; to countervail; to equiponderate; to balance.

Counterbalance Coun"ter*bal`ance (koun"t?r-b?l`ans), n. A weight, power, or agency, acting against or balancing another; as: (a) A mass of metal in one side of a driving wheel or fly wheel, to balance the weight of a crank pin, etc., on the opposite side of the wheel. (b) A counterpoise to balance the weight of anything, as of a drawbridge or a scale beam.

counterbore.c: Counterbore Coun"ter*bore` (-b?r`), n. 1. A flat-bottomed cylindrical enlargement of the mouth of a hole, usually of slight depth, as for receiving a cylindrical screw head.
Counterbore Coun`ter*bore" (koun`t?r-b?r"), v. t. To form a counterbore in, by boring, turning, or drilling; to enlarge, as a hole, by means of a counterbore.

counterbrace.c: Counterbrace Coun"ter*brace`, v. t. 1. (Naut.) To brace in opposite directions; as, to counterbrace the yards, i. e., to brace the head yards one way and the after yards another.

counterbuff.c: Counterbuff Coun`ter*buff" (koun`t?r-b?f"), v. t. To strike or drive back or in an opposite direction; to stop by a blow or impulse in front. Dryden.
Counterbuff Coun"ter*buff` (koun"t?r-b?f`), n. A blow in an opposite direction; a stroke that stops motion or cause a recoil.

countercast.c: Countercast Coun"ter*cast` (koun"t?r-k?st`), n. A trick; a delusive contrivance. [Obs.] Spenser.

countercaster.c: Countercaster Coun"ter*cast`er (-?r), n. A caster of accounts; a reckoner; a bookkeeper; -- used contemptuously.

counterchange.c: Counterchange Coun`ter*change" (koun`tẽr*chānj), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterchanged (-ch?njd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Counterchanging.] 1. To give and receive; to cause to change places; to exchange.

countercharm.c: Countercharm Coun`ter*charm" (koun`t?r-ch?rm"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countercharmed (-ch?rmd`); p. pr. & vb. n. Countercharming.] To destroy the effect of a charm upon.
Countercharm Coun"ter*charm` (koun"t?r-ch?rm`), n. That which has the power of destroying the effect of a charm.

countercheck.c: Countercheck Coun`ter*check" (koun`t?r-ch?k"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterchecked (-ch?ckt"); p. pr. & vb. n. Counterchecking.] To oppose or check by some obstacle; to check by a return check.
Countercheck Coun"ter*check` (koun"t?r-ch?k`), n. 1. A check; a stop; a rebuke, or censure to check a reprover.

counterclaim.c: Counterclaim Coun"ter*claim` (-klām`), n. (Law) A claim made by a person as an offset to a claim made on him.

countercouchant.c: Counter-couchant Coun"ter-couch`ant (koun"tẽr*kouch"aint), a. (Her.) Lying down, with their heads in opposite directions; -- said of animals borne in a coat of arms.

countercourant.c: Counter-courant Coun"ter-cou*rant" (-k??-r?nt"), a. (Her.) Running in opposite directions; -- said of animals borne in a coast of arms.

countercurrent.c: Countercurrent Coun"ter*cur`rent (koun"t?r-k?r`-rent), a. Running in an opposite direction.
Countercurrent Coun"ter*cur`rent, n. A current running in an opposite direction to the main current.

counterdraw.c: Counterdraw Coun`ter*draw" (koun`tẽr*drä"), v. t. [imp. Counterdrew (-drü"); p. p. Counterdrawn (-dr?n"); p. pr. & vb. n. Counterdrawing.] To copy, as a design or painting, by tracing with a pencil on oiled paper, or other transparent substance.

counterfeit.c: Counterfeit Coun"ter*feit (koun"t?r-f?t), a. [F. contrefait, p. p. of contrefaire to counterfeit; contre (L. contra) + faire to make, fr. L. facere. See Counter, adv., and Fact.]
Counterfeit Coun"ter*feit, n. 1. That which resembles or is like another thing; a likeness; a portrait; a counterpart.
Counterfeit Coun"ter*feit, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterfeited; p. pr. & vb. n. Counterfeiting.] 1. To imitate, or put on a semblance of; to mimic; as, to counterfeit the voice of another person.
Counterfeit Coun"ter*feit, v. i. 1. To carry on a deception; to dissemble; to feign; to pretend.

counterfeiter.c: Counterfeiter Coun"ter*feit`er (-f?t`?r), n. 1. One who counterfeits; one who copies or imitates; especially, one who copies or forges bank notes or coin; a forger.

counterfesance.c: Counterfesance Coun"ter*fe`sance (-f?"zans), n. [OF. contrefaisance, fr. contrefaire. See Counterfeit, a.] The act of forging; forgery. [Obs.] [Written also counterfaisance.]

counterflory.c: Counterflory Coun"ter*flo`ry (-fl?`r?), a. [See Counterfleury.] (Her.) Adorned with flowers (usually fleurs-de-lis) so divided that the tops appear on one side and the bottoms on the others; -- said of any ordinary.

counterfort.c: Counterfort Coun"ter*fort` (-f?rt`), n. 1. (Fort.) A kind of buttress of masonry to strengthen a revetment wall.

countergage.c: Countergage Coun"ter*gage` (-gāj`), n. (Carp.) An adjustable gage, with double points for transferring measurements from one timber to another, as the breadth of a mortise to the place where the tenon is to be made. Knight.

counterglow.c: Counterglow Coun"ter*glow` (?), n. (Astron.) An exceedingly faint roundish or somewhat oblong nebulous light near the ecliptic and opposite the sun, best seen during September and October, when in the constellations Sagittarius and Pisces. Its cause is not yet understood. Called also Gegenschein.

counterguard.c: Counterguard Coun"ter*guard` (koun"tẽr*gärd`), n. (Fort.) A low outwork before a bastion or ravelin, consisting of two lines of rampart parallel to the faces of the bastion, and protecting them from a breaching fire.

counterirritation.c: Counterirritation Counterirritant Coun"ter*ir`ri*tant (-?r"r?-tant), n., Coun"ter*ir`ri*ta"tion, n. See Counter irritant, etc., under Counter, a.

counterirritate.c: Counterirritate Coun"ter*ir"ri*tate (koun"tẽr-?r"r?-t?t), v. t. (Med.) To produce counter irritation in; to treat with one morbid process for the purpose of curing another.

counterjumper.c: Counterjumper Coun"ter*jump`er (koun"tẽr-j?mp`?r), n. A salesman in a shop; a shopman; -- used contemptuously. [Slang]

counterlath.c: Counterlath Coun"ter*lath` (?), n. (Building) (a) A batten laid lengthwise between two rafters to afford a bearing for laths laid crosswise. (b) Any lath laid without actual measurement between two gauged laths. (c) Any of a series of laths nailed to the timbers to raise the sheet lathing above their surface to afford a key for plastering. (d) One of many laths used in preparing one side of a partition or framed wall, when the other side has been covered in and finished.

counterman.c: Counterman Coun"ter*man (koun"tẽr*main), n.; pl. Countermen (-mein). A man who attends at the counter of a shop to sell goods. [Eng.]

countermand.c: Countermand Coun`ter*mand" (koun`tẽr*mȧnd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countermanded; p. pr. & vb. n. Countermanding.] [F. contremander; contre (L. contra) + mander to command, fr. L. mandare. Cf. Mandate.] 1. To revoke (a former command); to cancel or rescind by giving an order contrary to one previously given; as, to countermand an order for goods.
Countermand Coun"ter*mand (koun"tẽr*mȧnd), n. A contrary order; revocation of a former order or command.

countermandable.c: Countermandable Coun`ter*mand"a*ble (-m?nd"?-b'l), a. Capable of being countermanded; revocable. Bacon.

countermarch.c: Countermarch Coun`ter*march" (koun`t?r-m?rch"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Countermarched (-m?rcht"); p. pr. & vb. n. Countermarching.] (Mil.) To march back, or to march in reversed order.
Countermarch Coun"ter*march` (koun"t?r-m?rch`), n. 1. A marching back; retrocession.

countermark.c: Countermark Coun"ter*mark` (-m?rk`), n. 1. A mark or token added to those already existing, in order to afford security or proof; as, an additional or special mark put upon a package of goods belonging to several persons, that it may not be opened except in the presence of all; a mark added to that of an artificer of gold or silver work by the Goldsmiths' Company of London, to attest the standard quality of the gold or silver; a mark added to an ancient coin or medal, to show either its change of value or that it was taken from an enemy.
Countermark Coun`ter*mark" (koun`tẽr*märk"), v. t. To apply a countermark to; as, to countermark silverware; to countermark a horse's teeth.

countermine.c: Countermine Coun"ter*mine` (koun"tẽr*mīn`), n. [Counter- + mine underground gallery: cf. F. contermine.] 1. (Mil.) An underground gallery excavated to intercept and destroy the mining of an enemy.

Countermine Coun`ter*mine" (koun`tẽr*mīn"), v. t. [Cf. F. contreminer.] [imp. & p. p. Countermined; p. pr. & vb. n. Countermining.] 1. (Mil.) To oppose by means of a countermine; to intercept with a countermine.
Countermine Coun`ter*mine", v. i. To make a countermine or counterplot; to plot secretly.

countermove.c: Countermove Coun`ter*move" (koun`t?r-m??v"), v. t. & i. To move in a contrary direction to.

countermovement.c: Countermovement Countermove { Coun"ter*move` (-m??v`), n. Coun"ter*move`ment (-ment). } A movement in opposition to another.

countermure.c: Countermure Coun"ter*mure` (-m?r`), n. [Counter- + mure: cf. F. contremur.] (Fort.) A wall raised behind another, to supply its place when breached or destroyed. [R.] Cf. Contramure. Knolles.
Countermure Coun`ter*mure" (koun`t?r-m?r"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countermured (-m?rd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Countermuring.] [Cf. F. contremurer.] To fortify with a wall behind another wall. [R.] Kyd.

counternatural.c: Counternatural Coun"ter*nat`u*ral (koun"t?r-n?t`?-ral; 135), a. Contrary to nature. [R.] Harvey.

counterpaly.c: Counter-paly Coun"ter-pa`ly (-p?`l?), a. [F. contre-palé.] (Her.) Paly, and then divided fesswise, so that each vertical piece is cut into two, having the colors used alternately or counterchanged. Thus the escutcheon in the illustration may also be blazoned paly of six per fess counterchanged argent and azure.

counterpane.c: Counterpane Coun"ter*pane` (koun"t?r-p?n`), n. [See Counterpoint, corrupted into counterpane, from the employment of pane-shaped figures in these coverlets. ] A coverlet for a bed, -- originally stitched or woven in squares or figures.

Counterpane Coun"ter*pane`, n. [OF. contrepan a pledge, security; contre + pan a skirt, also, a pawn or gage, F. pan a skirt. See Pane, and cf. Pawn.] (O. Law) A duplicate part or copy of an indenture, deed, etc., corresponding with the original; -- now called counterpart.

counterpart.c: Counterpart Coun"ter*part` (koun"tẽr*pärt`), n. 1. A part corresponding to another part; anything which answers, or corresponds, to another; a copy; a duplicate; a facsimile.

counterpassant.c: Counterpassant Coun"ter*pas`sant (-p?s"sant), a. [Counter- + passant: cf. F. contrepassant.] (Her.) Passant in opposite directions; -- said of two animals.

counterplead.c: Counterplead Coun`ter*plead" (koun`t?r-pl?d"), v. t. To plead the contrary of; to plead against; to deny.

counterplot.c: Counterplot Coun`ter*plot" (koun`t?r-pl?t"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterplotted; p. pr. & vb. n. Counterplotting.] To oppose, as another plot, by plotting; to attempt to frustrate, as a stratagem, by stratagem.
Counterplot Coun"ter*plot` (koun"tẽr-pl?t`), n. A plot or artifice opposed to another. L'Estrange.

counterpoint.c: Counterpoint Coun"ter*point` (koun"t?r-point`), n. [Counter- + point.] An opposite point [Obs.] Sir E. Sandys.

Counterpoint Coun"ter*point`, n. [F. contrepoint; cf. It. contrappunto. Cf. Contrapuntal.] (Mus.) (a) The setting of note against note in harmony; the adding of one or more parts to a given canto fermo or melody. (b) The art of polyphony, or composite melody, i. e., melody not single, but moving attended by one or more related melodies. (c) Music in parts; part writing; harmony; polyphonic music. See Polyphony.

Counterpoint Coun"ter*point`, n. [OF. contrepoincte, corruption of earlier counstepointe, countepointe, F. courtepointe, fr. L. culcita cushion, mattress (see Quilt, and cf. Cushion) + puncta, fem. p. p. of pungere to prick (see Point). The word properly meant a stitched quilt, with the colors broken one into another.] A coverlet; a cover for a bed, often stitched or broken into squares; a counterpane. See 1st Counterpane.

counterpoise.c: Counterpoise Coun"ter*poise` (koun"t?r-poiz`; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterpoised (-poizd`); p. pr. & vb. n. Counterpoising.] [OE. countrepesen, counterpeisen, F. contrepeser. See Counter, adv., and Poise, v. t. ] 1. To act against with equal weight; to equal in weight; to balance the weight of; to counterbalance.

Counterpoise Coun"ter*poise` (koun"t?r-poiz`), n. [OE. countrepese, OF. contrepois, F. contrepods. See Counter, adv., and Poise, n.] 1. A weight sufficient to balance another, as in the opposite scale of a balance; an equal weight.

counterponderate.c: Counterponderate Coun`ter*pon"der*ate (-p?n"d?r-?t), v. t. To equal in weight; to counterpoise; to equiponderate.

counterprove.c: Counterprove Coun`ter*prove" (koun`t?r-pr??v"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Counterproved (-pr??vd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Counterproving.] To take a counter proof of, or a copy in reverse, by taking an impression directly from the face of an original. See Counter proof, under Counter.

counterroll.c: Counter-roll Coun"ter-roll` (-r?l`), n. [Cf. Control.] (O. Eng. Law) A duplicate roll (record or account) kept by an officer as a check upon another officer's roll. Burrill.

counterrolment.c: Counterrolment Coun`ter*rol"ment (koun`tẽr-r?l"ment), n. A counter account. See Control. [Obs.] Bacon.

countersalient.c: Counter-salient Coun`ter-sa"li*ent (koun`tẽr-sā"lĭ*ei>nt or -sāl"yeint; 106), a. (Her.) Leaping from each other; -- said of two figures on a coat of arms.

counterscale.c: Counterscale Coun"ter*scale` (koun`tẽr-skāl`), n. Counterbalance; balance, as of one scale against another. [Obs.] Howell.

counterscarp.c: Counterscarp Coun"ter*scarp` (koun`tẽr*skärp`) n. [Counter- + scarp: cf. F. contrescarpe.] (Fort.) The exterior slope or wall of the ditch; -- sometimes, the whole covered way, beyond the ditch, with its parapet and glacis; as, the enemy have lodged themselves on the counterscarp.

counterseal.c: Counterseal Coun`ter*seal" (koun`tẽr*sēl"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countersealed (koun`tẽr*sēld"); p. pr. & vb. n. Countersealing.] To seal or ratify with another or others. Shak.

countersecure.c: Countersecure Coun`ter*se*cure" (-s?-k?r"), v. t. To give additional security to or for. Burke.

countershaft.c: Countershaft Coun"ter*shaft` (koun"t?r-sh?ft`), n. (Mach.) An intermediate shaft; esp., one which receives motion from a line shaft in a factory and transmits it to a machine.

countersign.c: Countersign Coun`ter*sign" (-s?n`; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countersigned (-s?nd`); p. pr. & vb. n. Countersigning.] [Counter- + sign: cf. F. contresigner.] To sign on the opposite side of (an instrument or writing); hence, to sign in addition to the signature of a principal or superior, in order to attest the authenticity of a writing.
Countersign Coun"ter*sign`, a. 1. The signature of a secretary or other officer to a writing signed by a principal or superior, to attest its authenticity.

countersink.c: Countersink Coun"ter*sink` (koun"tẽr*sĭṉk`; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countersunk (-sŭṉk`); p. pr. & vb. n. Countersinking.] 1. To chamfer or form a depression around the top of (a hole in wood, metal, etc.) for the reception of the head of a screw or bolt below the surface, either wholly or in part; as, to countersink a hole for a screw.
Countersink Coun"ter*sink`, n. 1. An enlargement of the upper part of a hole, forming a cavity or depression for receiving the head of a screw or bolt.

counterstand.c: Counterstand Coun"ter*stand` (-st?nd`), n. Resistance; opposition; a stand against.

counterstep.c: Counterstep Coun"ter*step` (koun"t?r-st?p`), n. A contrary method of procedure; opposite course of action.

counterstroke.c: Counterstroke Coun"ter*stroke` (-str?k`), n. A stroke or blow in return. Spenser.

countersunk.c: Countersunk Coun"ter*sunk` (-s?nk`), p. p. & a. from Countersink. 1. Chamfered at the top; -- said of a hole.

countersway.c: Countersway Coun"ter*sway` (-swā`), n. A swaying in a contrary direction; an opposing influence. [Obs.]

counterterm.c: Counterterm Coun"ter*term` (-t?rm`), n. A term or word which is the opposite of, or antithesis to, another; an antonym; -- the opposite of synonym; as, “foe” is the counterterm of “friend”. C. J. Smith.

countertime.c: Countertime Coun"ter*time` (-t?m`), n. 1. (Man.) The resistance of a horse, that interrupts his cadence and the measure of his manege, occasioned by a bad horseman, or the bad temper of the horse.

countertrippant.c: Countertrippant Coun"ter*trip`pant (-tr?p`pant), a. (Her.) Trippant in opposite directions. See Trippant.

counterturn.c: Counterturn Coun"ter*turn` (-t?rn`), n. The critical moment in a play, when, contrary to expectation, the action is embroiled in new difficulties. Dryden.

countervail.c: Countervail Coun`ter*vail" (koun`t?r-v?l"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Countervailed (-v?ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Countervailing.] [OF. contrevaloir; contre (L. contra) + valoir to avail, fr. L. valere to be strong, avail. See Vallant.] To act against with equal force, power, or effect; to thwart or overcome by such action; to furnish an equivalent to or for; to counterbalance; to compensate.
Countervail Coun"ter*vail` (koun"t?r-v?l`), n. Power or value sufficient to obviate any effect; equal weight, strength, or value; equivalent; compensation; requital. [Obs.]

counterview.c: Counterview Coun"ter*view` (koun"t?r-v?`), n. 1. An opposite or opposing view; opposition; a posture in which two persons front each other.

countervote.c: Countervote Coun`ter*vote" (koun`tẽr*vōt"), v. t. To vote in opposition to; to balance or overcome by voting; to outvote. Dr. J. Scott.

counterwait.c: Counterwait Coun`ter*wait" (koun`tẽr*wāt"), v. t. To wait or watch for; to be on guard against. [Obs.] Chaucer.

counterweigh.c: Counterweigh Coun`ter*weigh" (-wā"), v. t. To weigh against; to counterbalance.

counterwheel.c: Counterwheel Coun`ter*wheel" (-hwēl"), v. t. (Mil.) To cause to wheel or turn in an opposite direction.

counterwork.c: Counterwork Coun`ter*work" (-wûrk"), v. t. To work in opposition to; to counteract.

countess.c: Countess Count"ess (kount"?s), n.; pl. Countesses (-?s). [F. comtesse. See Count a nobleman.] The wife of an earl in the British peerage, or of a count in the Continental nobility; also, a lady possessed of the same dignity in her own right. See the Note under Count.

countingroom.c: Countingroom Countinghouse { Count"ing*house` (kount"?ng-hous`), Count"ing*room` (kount"?ng-r??m`), } n. [See Count, v.] The house or room in which a merchant, trader, or manufacturer keeps his books and transacts business; the offices used by the accountants of a business.

countless.c: Countless Count"less (-l?s), a. Incapable of being counted; not ascertainable; innumerable.

countor.c: Countor Count"or (kount"?r), n. [From Count, v. t. (in sense 4).] (O. Eng. Law) An advocate or professional pleader; one who counted for his client, that is, orally pleaded his cause. [Obs.] Burrill.

countourhouse.c: Countourhouse Countour { Coun*tour" (k??n-t??r"), Coun*tour"house` (-hous`), } n. [See 2d Counter.] A merchant's office; a countinghouse. [Obs.] Chaucer.

countreplete.c: Countreplete Coun`tre*plete" (-pl?t"), v. t. [Countre- + plete to plead.] To counterplead. [Obs.] Chaucer.

countretaille.c: Countretaille Coun"tre*taille` (koun"t?r-t?l`), n. [F. contretaille; contre (L. contra) + taille cut. See Tally.] A counter tally; correspondence (in sound). [Obs.]

countrified.c: Countrified Coun"tri*fied (kŭn"trĭ*fīd), p. a. [Also spelled countryfied.] Having the appearance and manners of a rustic; rude; as, countrified clothes.

countrify.c: Countrify Coun"tri*fy (k?n"tr?-f?), v. t. To give a rural appearance to; to cause to appear rustic. Lamb.

country.c: Country Coun"try (k?n"tr?), n.; pl. Countries (-tr?z). [F. contrée, LL. contrata, fr. L. contra over against, on the opposite side. Cf. Counter, adv., Contra.] 1. A tract of land; a region; the territory of an independent nation; (as distinguished from any other region, and with a personal pronoun) the region of one's birth, permanent residence, or citizenship.
Country Coun"try, a. 1. Pertaining to the regions remote from a city; rural; rustic; as, a country life; a country town; the country party, as opposed to city.
Country bank Coun"try bank. (Banking) A national bank not in a reserve city. [Colloq., U. S.]
Country club Coun"try club. A club usually located in the suburbs or vicinity of a city or town and devoted mainly to outdoor sports, and usually having an attached golf course.
Country cousin Coun"try cousin. A relative from the country visiting the city and unfamiliar with city manners and sights.
Country seat Coun"try seat` (k?n"tr? s?t`). A dwelling in the country, used as a place of retirement from the city.

countrybase.c: Country-base Coun"try-base` (-b?s`), n. Same as Prison base.

countrydance.c: Country-dance Coun"try-dance` (-d?ns`), n. [Prob. an adaptation of contradance.] See Contradance.

countryman.c: Countryman Coun"try*man (kŭn"trĭ-main), n.; pl. Countrymen (-mein). 1. An inhabitant or native of a region. Shak.

countryside.c: Countryside Coun"try*side` (-s?d`), n. A particular rural district; a country neighborhood. [Eng.] W. Black. Blackmore.

countrywoman.c: Countrywoman Coun"try*wom`an (-w??m`an), n.; pl. Countrywomen (-w?m`?n). A woman born, or dwelling, in the country, as opposed to the city; a woman born or dwelling in the same country with another native or inhabitant. Shak.

countwheel.c: Count-wheel Count"-wheel` (kount"hw?l`), n. The wheel in a clock which regulates the number of strokes.

county.c: County Coun"ty (koun"ty̆), n.; pl. Counties (-tĭz). [F. comté, fr. LL. comitatus. See Count.] 1. An earldom; the domain of a count or earl. [Obs.]

coup.c: Coup ‖Coup (kōo), n. [F., fr.L. colaphus a cuff, Gr. ko`lafos.] 1. A sudden stroke delivered with promptness and force; -- used also in various ways to convey the idea of an unexpected, clever, and successful tactic or stratagem.
Coup Coup. v. i. To make a coup.

coupe.c: Coupe ‖Cou`pé" (kōo`pa"), n. [F., fr. coupé, p. p. of couper to cut. See Coppice.] 1. The front compartment of a French diligence; also, the front compartment (usually for three persons) of a car or carriage on British railways.

couped.c: Couped Couped (kōopt), a. [F. couper to cut.] (Her.) Cut off smoothly, as distinguished from erased; -- used especially for the head or limb of an animal. See Erased.

coupee.c: Coupee Cou*pee" (kōo*pē"; F. kōo`pa"), n. [F. coupé, n., properly p. p. of couper to cut. Cf. Coupé, Coopee.] A motion in dancing, when one leg is a little bent, and raised from the floor, and with the other a forward motion is made. Chambers.

coupegorge.c: Coupe-gorge ‖Coupe`-gorge" (kōop`gôrzh"), n. [F., cut throat.] (Mil.) Any position giving the enemy such advantage that the troops occupying it must either surrender or be cut to pieces. Farrow.

couple.c: Couple Cou"ple (kŭp"'l), n. [F. couple, fr. L. copula a bond, band; co- + apere, aptum, to join. See Art, a., and cf. Copula.] 1. That which joins or links two things together; a bond or tie; a coupler. [Obs.]
Couple Cou"ple, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coupled (kŭp"'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Coupling (kŭp"lĭng).] [F. coupler, fr. L. copulare. See Couple, n., and cf. Copulate, Cobble, v.]
Couple Cou"ple, v. i. To come together as male and female; to copulate. [Obs.] Milton. Bacon.

couplebeggar.c: Couple-beggar Cou"ple-beg`gar (-b?g`g?r), n. One who makes it his business to marry beggars to each other. Swift.

coupleclose.c: Couple-close Cou"ple-close` (kŭp"'l*klōs`), n.; pl. Couple-closes (kŭp"'l*klō"sĕz). 1. (Her.) A diminutive of the chevron, containing one fourth of its surface. Couple-closes are generally borne one on each side of a chevron, and the blazoning may then be either a chevron between two couple-closes or chevron cottised.

couplement.c: Couplement Cou"ple*ment (k?p"'l-ment), n. [Cf. OF. couplement.] Union; combination; a coupling; a pair. [Obs.] Shak.

coupler.c: Coupler Coup"ler (k?p"l?r), n. One who couples; that which couples, as a link, ring, or shackle, to connect cars.

couplet.c: Couplet Coup"let (-l?t), n. [F. couplet, dim. of couple. See Couple, n. ] Two taken together; a pair or couple; especially two lines of verse that rhyme with each other.

coupling.c: Coupling Coup"ling (-l?ng), n. 1. The act of bringing or coming together; connection; sexual union.

coupon.c: Coupon Cou"pon (k??"p?n; F. k??`p?n"), n. [F., fr. couper to cut, cut off. See Coppice.] 1. (Com.) A certificate of interest due, printed at the bottom of transferable bonds (state, railroad, etc.), given for a term of years, designed to be cut off and presented for payment when the interest is due; an interest warrant.

coupstick.c: Coupstick Coup"stick` (kōo"stĭk`), n. [Coup + stick.] A stick or switch used among some American Indians in making or counting a coup.

coupure.c: Coupure ‖Cou*pure" (k??-p?r"), n. [F., fr. couper to cut.] (Fort.) A passage cut through the glacis to facilitate sallies by the besieged. Wilhelm.

courage.c: Courage Cour"age (kŭr"aj; 48), n. [OE. corage heart, mind, will, courage, OF. corage, F. courage, fr. a LL. derivative of L. cor heart. See Heart.] 1. The heart; spirit; temper; disposition. [Obs.]
Courage Cour"age, v. t. To inspire with courage; to encourage. [Obs.]

courageous.c: Courageous Cour*a"geous (k?r-?"j?s), a. [F. courageux.] Possessing, or characterized by, courage; brave; bold.

courageously.c: Courageously Cour*a"geous*ly, adv. In a courageous manner.

courageousness.c: Courageousness Cour*a"geous*ness, n. The quality of being courageous; courage.

courant.c: Courant Cou*rant" (k??-r?nt"), a. [F., p. pr. of courir to run, L. currere. Cf. Current.] (Her.) Represented as running; -- said of a beast borne in a coat of arms.
Courant Cou*rant" (k??-r?nt"), n. [F. courante, fr. courant, p. pr.] 1. A piece of music in triple time; also, a lively dance; a coranto.

couranto.c: Couranto Cou*ran"to (-r?n"t?), n. A sprightly dance; a coranto; a courant.

courap.c: Courap Cou*rap" (k??-r?p), n. (Med.) A skin disease, common in India, in which there is perpetual itching and eruption, esp. of the groin, breast, armpits, and face.

courb.c: Courb Courb (k??rb), a. [F. courbe, fr. L. curvus. See Curve, a.] Curved; rounded. [Obs.]
Courb Courb (k??rb), v. i. [F. courber. See Curs.] To bend; to stop; to bow. [Obs.]

courbaril.c: Courbaril Cour"ba*ril (k??r"b?-r?l), n. [F. courbaril, from a South American word.] See Animé, n.

courche.c: Courche Courche (k??rsh), n. [Cf. Kerchief.] A square piece of linen used formerly by women instead of a cap; a kerchief. [Scot.] [Written also curch.] Jamieson.

courier.c: Courier Cou"ri*er (k??"r?-?r), n. [F. courrier, fr. courre, courir, to run, L. currere. See Course, Current.] 1. A messenger sent with haste to convey letters or dispatches, usually on public business.

courlan.c: Courlan Cour"lan (k??r"l?n), n. (Zool.) A South American bird, of the genus Aramus, allied to the rails.

course.c: Course Course (kōrs), n. [F. cours, course, L. cursus, fr. currere to run. See Current.] 1. The act of moving from one point to another; progress; passage.
Course Course, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coursed (k?rst)); p. pr. & vb. n. Coursing.] 1. To run, hunt, or chase after; to follow hard upon; to pursue.
Course Course, v. i. 1. To run as in a race, or in hunting; to pursue the sport of coursing; as, the sportsmen coursed over the flats of Lancashire.

coursed.c: Coursed Coursed (k?rst), a. 1. Hunted; as, a coursed hare.

courser.c: Courser Cours"er (k?rs"?r), n. [F. coursier.] 1. One who courses or hunts.

coursey.c: Coursey Cour"sey (k?r"s?), n. [Cf. OF. corsie, coursie, passage way to the stern. See Course, n. ] (Naut.)A space in the galley; a part of the hatches. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

coursing.c: Coursing Cours"ing (k?rs"?ng), n. The pursuit or running game with dogs that follow by sight instead of by scent.

court.c: Court Court (kōrt), n. [OF. court, curt, cort, F. cour, LL. cortis, fr. L. cohors, cors, chors, gen. cohortis, cortis, chortis, an inclosure, court, thing inclosed, crowd, throng; co- + a root akin to Gr. chorto`s inclosure, feeding place, and to E. garden, yard, orchard. See Yard, and cf. Cohort, Curtain.] 1. An inclosed space; a courtyard; an uncovered area shut in by the walls of a building, or by different building; also, a space opening from a street and nearly surrounded by houses; a blind alley.
Court Court, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Courted; p. pr. & vb. n. Courting.] 1. To endeavor to gain the favor of by attention or flattery; to try to ingratiate one's self with.
Court Court, v. i. 1. To play the lover; to woo; as, to go courting.
Court tennis Court" ten"nis (k?rt" t?n"n?s). See under Tennis.

courtbaron.c: Court-baron Court"-bar`on (-b?r`?n), n. (Law) An inferior court of civil jurisdiction, attached to a manor, and held by the steward; a baron's court; -- now fallen into disuse.

courtbred.c: Courtbred Court"bred` (-br?d`), a. Bred, or educated, at court; polished; courtly.

courtcraft.c: Court-craft Court"-craft` (k?rt"kr?ft`), n. The artifices, intrigues, and plottings, at courts.

courtcupboard.c: Court-cupboard Court"-cup`board (-k?b`b?rd), n. A movable sideboard or buffet, on which plate and other articles of luxury were displayed on special ocasions. [Obs.]

courteous.c: Courteous Cour"te*ous (k?r"t?-?s; 277), a. [OE. cortais, corteis, cortois, rarely corteous, OF. corties, corteis, F. courtois. See Court.] Of courtlike manners; pertaining to, or expressive of, courtesy; characterized by courtesy; civil; obliging; well bred; polite; affable; complaisant.

courteously.c: Courteously Cour"te*ous*ly, adv. In a courteous manner.

courteousness.c: Courteousness Cour"te*ous*ness, n. The quality of being courteous; politeness; courtesy.

courtepy.c: Courtepy Cour"te*py (k??r"t?-p?), n. [D. kort short + pije a coarse cloth.] A short coat of coarse cloth. [Obs.]

courter.c: Courter Court"er (k?rt"?r), n. One who courts; one who plays the lover, or who solicits in marriage; one who flatters and cajoles. Sherwood.

courtesan.c: Courtesan Cour"te*san (k?r"t?-z?n; 277), n. [F. courtisane, fr. courtisan courtier, It. cortigiano; or directly fr. It. cortigiana, or Sp. cortesana. See Court.] A woman who prostitutes herself for hire; a prostitute; a harlot.

courtesy.c: Courtesy Cour"te*sy (k?r"t?-s?), n.; pl. Courtesies (-s?z). [OE. cortaisie, corteisie, courtesie, OF. curteisie, cortoisie, OF. curteisie, cortoisie, F. courtoisie, fr. curteis, corteis. See Courteous.] 1. Politeness; civility; urbanity; courtliness.

Courtesy Courte"sy (kûrt"sy̆), n. [See the preceding word.] An act of civility, respect, or reverence, made by women, consisting of a slight depression or dropping of the body, with bending of the knees. [Written also curtsy and curtsey.]

Courtesy Courte"sy, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Courtesied (-sĭd); p. pr. & vb. n. Courtesying.] To make a respectful salutation or movement of respect; esp. (with reference to women), to bow the body slightly, with bending of the knes.
Courtesy Courte"sy, v. t. To treat with civility. [Obs.]

courthouse.c: Courthouse Court"house` (kōrt"hous`), n. 1. A house in which established courts are held, or a house appropriated to courts and public meetings. [U.S.]

courtier.c: Courtier Court"ier (kōrt"yẽr), n. [From Court.] 1. One who is in attendance at the court of a prince; one who has an appointment at court.

courtiery.c: Courtiery Court"ier*y (-?), n. The manners of a courtier; courtliness. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

courtleet.c: Court-leet Court"-leet` (-l?t`), n. (Eng. Law) A court of record held once a year, in a particular hundred, lordship, or manor, before the steward of the leet. Blackstone.

courtlike.c: Courtlike Court"like` (-l?k`), a. After the manner of a court; elegant; polite; courtly.

courtliness.c: Courtliness Court"li*ness (-l?-n?s), n. [From Courtly.] The quality of being courtly; elegance or dignity of manners.

courtling.c: Courtling Court"ling (-l?ng), n. [Court + -ling.] A sycophantic courtier. B. Jonson.

courtly.c: Courtly Court"ly (-l?), a. [From Court.] 1. Relating or belonging to a court.
Courtly Court"ly, adv. In the manner of courts; politely; gracefully; elegantly.

courtmartial.c: Court-martial Court`-mar"tial (k?rt`m?r"shal), n.; pl. Courts-martial (k?rts`-). A court consisting of military or naval officers, for the trial of one belonging to the army or navy, or of offenses against military or naval law.
Court-martial Court`-mar"tial, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Court-martialed (-shald); p. pr. & vb. n. Court-martialing.] To subject to trial by a court-martial.

courtplaster.c: Court-plaster Court"-plas`ter (k?rt"pl?s`t?r), n. Sticking plaster made by coating taffeta or silk on one side with some adhesive substance, commonly a mixture of isinglass and glycerin.

courtship.c: Courtship Court"ship (k?rt"sh?p), n. 1. The act of paying court, with the intent to solicit a favor. Swift.

courtyard.c: Courtyard Court"yard (k?rt"y?rd`), n. A court or inclosure attached to a house.

couscous.c: Couscous Cous"cous` (k??s"k??s`), n. A kind of food used by the natives of Western Africa, made of millet flour with flesh, and leaves of the baobab; -- called also lalo.

couscousou.c: Couscousou Cous`cou*sou" (kōos`kōo*sōo"), n. A favorite dish in Barbary. See Couscous.

cousin.c: Cousin Cous"in (kŭz"'n), n. [F. cousin, LL. cosinus, cusinus, contr. from L. consobrinus the child of a mother's sister, cousin; con- + sobrinus a cousin by the mother's side, a form derived fr. soror (for sosor) sister. See Sister, and cf. Cozen, Coz.] 1. One collaterally related more remotely than a brother or sister; especially, the son or daughter of an uncle or aunt.

cousinage.c: Cousinage Cous"in*age (-?j), n. [F. cousinage, OF., also, cosinage. Cf. Cosinage, Cozenage.] Relationship; kinship. [Obs.] Wyclif.

cousingerman.c: Cousin-german Cous"in-ger"man (-j?r"man), n. [Cousin + german closely akin.] A first cousin. See Note under Cousin, 1.

cousinhood.c: Cousinhood Cous"in*hood (-h??d), n. The state or condition of a cousin; also, the collective body of cousins; kinsfolk.

cousinly.c: Cousinly Cous"in*ly, a. Like or becoming a cousin.

cousinry.c: Cousinry Cous"in*ry (k?z"'n-r?), n. A body or collection of cousins; the whole number of persons who stand in the relation of cousins to a given person or persons.

cousinship.c: Cousinship Cous"in*ship, n. The relationship of cousins; state of being cousins; cousinhood. G. Eliot.

coussinet.c: Coussinet Cous"si*net` (k??s"s?-n?t`), n. [F., dim. of coussin cushion. See Cushionet.] (Arch.) (a) A stone placed on the impost of a pier for receiving the first stone of an arch. (b) That part of the Ionic capital between the abacus and quarter round, which forms the volute. Gwilt.

couteau.c: Couteau Cou*teau" (k??-t?"), n. [F.] A knife; a dagger.

couth.c: Couth Couth (k??th), imp. & p. p. of Can. [See Can, and cf. Uncouth.] Could; was able; knew or known; understood. [Obs.]

couvade.c: Couvade ‖Cou`vade" (kōo`vȧd"), n. [F., fr. couver. See Covey.] A custom, among certain barbarous tribes, that when a woman gives birth to a child her husband takes to his bed, as if ill.

couveuse.c: Couveuse ‖Cou`veuse" (?), n. [F.] (Med.) An incubator for sickly infants, esp. those prematurely born.

covariant.c: Covariant Co*va"ri*ant (k?-v?"r?-aint), n. (Higher Alg.) A function involving the coefficients and the variables of a quantic, and such that when the quantic is lineally transformed the same function of the new variables and coefficients shall be equal to the old function multiplied by a factor. An invariant is a like function involving only the coefficients of the quantic.

cove.c: Cove Cove (kōv), n. [AS. cofa room; akin to G. koben pigsty, orig., hut, Icel. kofi hut, and perh. to E. cobalt.]
Cove Cove, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coved (k?vd); p. pr. & vb. n. Coving.] (Arch.) To arch over; to build in a hollow concave form; to make in the form of a cove.
Cove Cove, v. t. [CF. F. couver, It. covare. See Covey.] To brood, cover, over, or sit over, as birds their eggs. [Obs.]
Cove Cove, n. [A gypsy word, covo that man, covi that woman.] A boy or man of any age or station. [Slang]

covellite.c: Covellite Covelline { Co*vel"line (k?-v?l"l?n), Co*vel"lite } (-l?t), n. [After Covelli, the discoverer.] (Min.) A native sulphide of copper, occuring in masses of a dark blue color; -- hence called indigo copper.

covenable.c: Covenable Cov"e*na*ble (k?v"?-n?-b'l), a. [OF. covenable, F. convenable. See Covenant.] Fit; proper; suitable. [Obs.] “A covenable day.” Wyclif (Mark vi. 21).

covenably.c: Covenably Cov"e*na*bly (k?v"?-n?-bly), adv. Fitly; suitably. [Obs.] “Well and covenably.” Chaucer.

covenant.c: Covenant Cov"e*nant (k?v"?-nant), n. [OF. covenant, fr. F. & OF. convenir to agree, L. convenire. See Convene.]

Covenant Cov"e*nant (k?v"?-n?nt), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Covenanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Covenanting.] To agree (with); to enter into a formal agreement; to bind one's self by contract; to make a stipulation.
Covenant Cov"e*nant, v. t. To grant or promise by covenant.

covenantee.c: Covenantee Cov`e*nan*tee" (k?v`?-nan-t?"), n. (Law) The person in whose favor a covenant is made.

covenanter.c: Covenanter Cov"e*nant*er (k?v"?-n?nt-?r), n. 1. One who makes a covenant.

covenanting.c: Covenanting Cov"e*nant*ing, a. Belonging to a covenant. Specifically, belonging to the Scotch Covenanters.

covenantor.c: Covenantor Cov"e*nant*or` (-?r`), n. (Law) The party who makes a covenant. Burrill.

covenous.c: Covenous Cov"e*nous (k?v"?-n?s), a. See Covinous, and Covin.

covent.c: Covent Cov"ent (k?v"ent), n. [OF. covent, F. couvent. See Convent.] A convent or monastery. [Obs.] Bale.

coventry.c: Coventry Cov"en*try (k?v"en-tr?), n. A town in the county of Warwick, England.

cover.c: Cover Cov"er (k?v"?r), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Covered (-?rd); p. pr. & vb. n. Covering.] [OF. covrir, F. couvrir, fr. L. cooperire; co- + operire to cover; probably fr. ob towards, over + the root appearing in aperire to open. Cf. Aperient, Overt, Curfew.] 1. To overspread the surface of (one thing) with another; as, to cover wood with paint or lacquer; to cover a table with a cloth.
Cover Cov"er (k?v"?r), n. 1. Anything which is laid, set, or spread, upon, about, or over, another thing; an envelope; a lid; as, the cover of a book.
Cover Cov"er, v. i. To spread a table for a meal; to prepare a banquet. [Obs.] Shak.
Cover crop Cov"er crop. A catch crop planted, esp. in orchards. as a protection to the soil in winter, as well as for the benefit of the soil when plowed under in spring.

coverchief.c: Coverchief Cov"er*chief (chēf), n. [See Kerchief.] A covering for the head. [Obs.] Chaucer.

covercle.c: Covercle Cov"er*cle (k?v"?r-k'l), n. [OF. covercle, F. couvercle, fr. L. cooperculum fr. cooperire. See cover] A small cover; a lid. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

covered.c: Covered Cov"ered (k?v"?rd), a. Under cover; screened; sheltered; not exposed; hidden.

coverer.c: Coverer Cov"er*er (-?r), n. One who, or that which, covers.

covering.c: Covering Cov"er*ing, n. Anything which covers or conceals, as a roof, a screen, a wrapper, clothing, etc.

coverlet.c: Coverlet Cov"er*let (k?v"?r-l?t), n. [F. couvre-lit; couvrir to cover + lit bed, fr. L. lectus bed. See Cover.] The uppermost cover of a bed or of any piece of furniture.

coverpoint.c: Cover-point Cov"er-point` (-point!), n. The fielder in the games of cricket and lacrosse who supports “point.”

coversed.c: Coversed sine Co*versed" sine (k?-v?rst" s?n`). [Co- (=co- in co- sine) + versed sine.] (Geom.) The versed sine of the complement of an arc or angle. See Illust. of Functions.

covershame.c: Cover-shame Cov"er-shame` (-sh?m`), n. Something used to conceal infamy. [Obs.] Dryden.

coverside.c: Coverside Cov"er*side` (?), n. A region of country having covers; a hunting country.

covert.c: Covert Cov"ert (k?v"?rt), a. [OF. covert, F. couvert, p. p. of couvrir. See Cover, v. t.] 1. Covered over; private; hid; secret; disguised.
Covert Cov"ert, n. [OF. See Covert, a.] 1. A place that covers and protects; a shelter; a defense.
Covert baron Cov"ert bar`on (b?r`?n). (Law) Under the protection of a husband; married. Burrill.

covertly.c: Covertly Cov"ert*ly, adv. Secretly; in private; insidiously.

coverture.c: Coverture Cov"er*ture (k?v"?r-t?r; 135), n. [OF. coverture,F.couverture.] 1. Covering; shelter; defense; hiding.

covet.c: Covet Cov"et (k?v"?t), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Covered; p. pr. & vb. n. Coveting.] [OF. coveitier, covoitier, F. convoiter, from a derivative fr. L. cupere to desire; cf. Skr. kup to become excited. Cf. Cupidity.]
Covet Cov"et, v. i. To have or indulge inordinate desire.

covetable.c: Covetable Cov"et*a*ble (k?v"?t-?-b'l), a. That may be coveted; desirable.

covetise.c: Covetise Cov"et*ise (-?s), n. [OF. coveitise, F. convoitise. See Covet, v. t. ] Avarice. [Obs.] Spenser.

covetous.c: Covetous Cov"et*ous (k?v"?t-?s), a. [OF. coveitos, F. convoiteux. See Covet, v. t.] 1. Very desirous; eager to obtain; -- used in a good sense. [Archaic]

covetously.c: Covetously Cov"et*ous*ly, adv. In a covetous manner.

covey.c: Covey Cov"ey (k?v"?), n. [OF. cov?e, F. couv?e, fr. cover, F. couver, to sit or brood on, fr. L. cubare to lie down; cf. E. incubate. See Cubit, and cf. Cove to brood.] 1. A brood or hatch of birds; an old bird with her brood of young; hence, a small flock or number of birds together; -- said of game; as, a covey of partridges. Darwin.
Covey Cov"ey, v. i. To brood; to incubate. [Obs.]
Covey Cov"ey, n. A pantry. [Prov. Eng.] Parker.

covin.c: Covin Cov"in (k?v"?n), n. [OF. covine, covaine, fr. covenir to agree. See Covenant.] 1. (Law) A collusive agreement between two or more persons to prejudice a third.

coving.c: Coving Cov"ing (?), n. (Arch.) (a) A cove or series of coves, as the concaved surface under the overhang of a projecting upper story. (b) The splayed jambs of a flaring fireplace.

covinous.c: Covinous Cov"in*ous (k?v"?n-?s), a. (Law) Deceitful; collusive; fraudulent; dishonest.

cow.c: Cow Cow, n.; pl. Cows (kouz); old pl. Kine (kīn). [OE. cu, cou, AS. cū; akin to D. koe, G. kuh, OHG. kuo, Icel. kȳr, Dan. & Sw. ko, L. bos ox, cow, Gr. boy^s, Skr. gō. √223. Cf. Beef, Bovine, Bucolic, Butter, Nylghau.]
Cow Cow (kou), n. [See Cowl a hood.] A chimney cap; a cowl

Cow Cow, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cowed (koud); p. pr. & vb. n. Cowing.] [Cf. Icel. kuga, Sw. kufva to check, subdue, Dan. kue. Cf. Cuff, v. t.] To depress with fear; to daunt the spirits or courage of; to overawe.
Cow Cow, n. [Prob. from same root as cow, v. t.] (Mining) A wedge, or brake, to check the motion of a machine or car; a chock. Knight.
Cow parsley Cow" pars`ley (kou` p?rs`l?). (Bot.) An umbelliferous plant of the genus Chærophyllum (Chærophyllum temulum and Chærophyllum sylvestre).
Cow parsnip Cow" pars`nip (-n?p). (Bot.) A coarse umbelliferous weed of the genus Heracleum (Heracleum sphondylium in England, and Heracleum lanatum in America).

Cow tree Cow" tree` (kou" tr?`). [Cf. SP. palo de vaca.] (Bot.) A tree (Galactodendron utile or Brosimum Galactodendron) of South America, which yields, on incision, a nourishing fluid, resembling milk.

cowalker.c: Cowalker Co`walk"er (?), n. A phantasmic or “astral” body deemed to be separable from the physical body and capable of acting independently; a doppelgänger.

cowan.c: Cowan Cow"an (kou"ain), n. [Cf. OF. couillon a coward, a cullion.] One who works as a mason without having served a regular apprenticeship. [Scot.]

coward.c: Coward Cow"ard (kou"?rd), a. [OF. couard, coard, coart, n. and adj., F. couard, fr. OF. coe, coue, tail, F. queue (fr. L. coda, a form of cauda tail) + -ard; orig., short-tailed, as an epithet of the hare, or perh., turning tail, like a scared dog. Cf. Cue, Queue, Caudal.] 1. (Her.) Borne in the escutcheon with his tail doubled between his legs; -- said of a lion.
Coward Cow"ard, n. A person who lacks courage; a timid or pusillanimous person; a poltroon.
Coward Cow"ard, v. t. To make timorous; to frighten. [Obs.]

cowardice.c: Cowardice Cow"ard*ice (-ĭs), n. [F. couardise, fr. couard. See Coward.] Want of courage to face danger; extreme timidity; pusillanimity; base fear of danger or hurt; lack of spirit.

cowardish.c: Cowardish Cow"ard*ish, a. Cowardly. [Obs.] “A base and a cowardish mind.” Robynson (More's Utopia).

cowardize.c: Cowardize Cow"ard*ize (-?z), v. t. To render cowardly. [Obs.]

cowardly.c: Cowardly Cow"ard*ly, a. 1. Wanting courage; basely or weakly timid or fearful; pusillanimous; spiritless.
Cowardly Cow"ard*ly, adv. In the manner of a coward. Spenser.

cowbane.c: Cowbane Cow"bane` (kou"bān`), n. (Bot.) A poisonous umbelliferous plant; in England, the Cicuta virosa; in the United States, the Cicuta maculata and the Archemora rigida. See Water hemlock.

cowberry.c: Cowberry Cow"ber`ry (-bĕr`ry̆), n.; pl. Cowberries (-rĭz). (Bot.) A species of Vaccinium (Vaccinium Vitis-idæa), which bears acid red berries which are sometimes used in cookery; -- locally called mountain cranberry.

cowbird.c: Cowbird Cow"bird` (-bẽrd`), n. (Zool.) The cow blackbird (Molothrus ater), an American starling. Like the European cuckoo, it builds no nest, but lays its eggs in the nests of other birds; -- so called because frequently associated with cattle.

cowblakes.c: Cowblakes Cow"blakes` (-blāks`), n. pl. Dried cow dung used as fuel.[Prov. Eng.] Simmonds.

cowboy.c: Cowboy Cow"boy` (-boi`), n. 1. A cattle herder; a drover; specifically, one of an adventurous class of herders and drovers on the plains of the Western and Southwestern United States.

cowcatcher.c: Cowcatcher Cow"catch`er (-k?ch`?r), n. A strong inclined frame, usually of wrought-iron bars, in front of a locomotive engine, for catching or throwing off obstructions on a railway, as cattle; the pilot. [U.S.]

cower.c: Cower Cow"er (kou"ẽr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Cowered (kou"ẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Cowering.] [Cf. Icel. kera to doze, liequiet, Sw. kura, Dan. kure, G. kauern to cower, W. cwrian.] To stoop by bending the knees; to crouch; to squat; hence, to quail; to sink through fear.
Cower Cow"er (kou"ẽr), v. t. To cherish with care. [Obs.]

cowfish.c: Cowfish Cow"fish` (kou"fĭsh`), n. (Zool.) (a) The grampus. (b) A California dolphin (Tursiops Gillii). (c) A marine plectognath fish (Ostracoin quadricorne, and allied species), having two projections, like horns, in front; -- called also cuckold, coffer fish, trunkfish.

cowhage.c: Cowhage Cow"hage (kou"haj), n. [Cf. Hind. kawānch, koānch.] (Bot.) A leguminous climbing plant of the genus Mucuna, having crooked pods covered with sharp hairs, which stick to the fingers, causing intolerable itching. The spiculæ are sometimes used in medicine as a mechanical vermifuge. [Written also couhage, cowage, and cowitch.]

cowherd.c: Cowherd Cow"herd` (-h?rd`), n. [AS. cūhyrde; cū cow + hyrde a herder.] One whose occupation is to tend cows.

cowhide.c: Cowhide Cow"hide` (-h?d`), n. 1. The hide of a cow.
Cowhide Cow"hide`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cowhided; p. pr. & vb. n. Cowhiding.] To flog with a cowhide.

cowish.c: Cowish Cow"ish (kou"ĭsh), a. [From Cow, v. t.] Timorous; fearful; cowardly. [R.] Shak.
Cowish Cow"ish, n. (Bot.) An umbelliferous plant (Peucedanum Cous) with edible tuberous roots, found in Oregon. [Written also cous.]

cowl.c: Cowl Cowl (koul), n. [AS. cuhle, cugle, cugele; cf. dial. G. kogel, gugel, OF. coule, goule; all fr. LL. cuculla, cucullus, fr. L. cucullus cap, hood; perh. akin to celare to conceal, cella cell. Cf. Cucullate.] 1. A monk's hood; -- usually attached to the gown. The name was also applied to the hood and garment together.
Cowl Cowl, n. [Cf. OF. cuvele, cuvel, dim. of F. cuve tub, vat, fr. L. cupa. See Cup.] A vessel carried on a pole between two persons, for conveyance of water. Johnson.

cowled.c: Cowled Cowled (kould), a. Wearing a cowl; hooded; as, a cowled monk. “That cowled churchman.” Emerson.

cowleech.c: Cowleech Cow"leech` (kou"l?ch`), n. [2d cow + leech a physician.] One who heals diseases of cows; a cow doctor.

cowleeching.c: Cowleeching Cow"leech`ing, n. Healing the distemper of cows.

cowlick.c: Cowlick Cow"lick` (-l?k`), n. A tuft of hair turned up or awry (usually over the forehead), as if licked by a cow.

cowlstaff.c: Cowlstaff Cowl"staff` (koul"st?f`), n. [Cowl a vessel + staff.] A staff or pole on which a vessel is supported between two persons. Suckling.

coworker.c: coworker co-worker co`-work"er, co`work"er (k?`w?rk"?r), n. One who works with another; a cooperator.

cowpea.c: Cowpea Cow"pea` (kou"pē`), n. 1. The seed of one or more leguminous plants of the genus Dolichos; also, the plant itself. Many varieties are cultivated in the southern part of the United States.

cowpers.c: Cowper's glands Cow"per's glands` (kou"p?rz gl?ndz`). [After the discoverer, William Cowper, an English surgeon.] (Anat.) Two small glands discharging into the male urethra.

cowpilot.c: Cow-pilot Cow"-pi`lot (kou"pī`lŭt), n. (Zool.) A handsomely banded, coral-reef fish, of Florida and the West Indies (Pomacentrus saxatilis); -- called also mojarra.

cowpox.c: Cowpox Cow"pox` (-pŏks`), n. (Med.) A pustular eruptive disease of the cow, which, when communicated to the human system, as by vaccination, protects from the smallpox; vaccinia; -- called also kinepox, cowpock, and kinepock. Dunglison.

cowquake.c: Cowquake Cow"quake` (-kwāk`), n. (Bot.) A genus of plants (Briza); quaking grass.

cowry.c: Cowry Cowrie { Cow"rie Cow"ry } (kou"ry̆), n.; pl. Cowries (-rĭz). [Hind. kaurī.] (Zool.) A marine shell of the genus Cypræa.

cowslip.c: Cowslip Cow"slip` (-slĭp`), n. [AS. cūslyppe, cūsloppe, prob. orig., cow's droppings. Cf. Slop, n.] (Bot.) 1. A common flower in England (Primula veris) having yellow blossoms and appearing in early spring. It is often cultivated in the United States.

cowslipped.c: Cowslipped Cow"slipped` (-slĭpt`), a. Adorned with cowslips. “Cowslipped lawns.” Keats.

cowweed.c: Cowweed Cow"weed" (-wEd`),, n. (Bot.) Same as Cow parsley.

cowwheat.c: Cowwheat Cow"wheat` (-hw?t`), n. (Bot.) A weed of the genus Melampyrum, with black seeds, found on European wheatfields.

cox.c: Cox Cox (k?ks), n. [OE. cokes. Cf. Coax.] A coxcomb; a simpleton; a gull. [Obs.]

coxa.c: Coxa ‖Cox"a (k?ks"?), n. [L., the hip.] (Zool.) The first joint of the leg of an insect or crustacean.

coxalgy.c: Coxalgy Coxalgia { ‖Cox*al"gi*a (-?l"j?-?), Cox"al`gy (k?ks"?l`j?), } n. [NL. coxalgia, fr. L. coxa hip. + Gr.??? pain: cf. F. coxalgie.] (Med.) Pain in the hip.

coxcomb.c: Coxcomb Cox"comb` (k?ks"k?m`), n. [A corrupted spelling of cock's comb.] 1. (a) A strip of red cloth notched like the comb of a cock, which licensed jesters formerly wore in their caps. (b) The cap itself.

coxcombical.c: Coxcombical Cox*comb"ic*al (k?ks-k?m"?-kal), a. Befitting or indicating a coxcomb; like a coxcomb; foppish; conceited. -- Cox*comb"ic*al*ly, adv.

coxcombly.c: Coxcombly Cox"comb"ly (k?ks"k?m`l?), a. like a coxcomb. [Obs.] “You coxcombly ass, you!” Beau. & Fl.

coxcombry.c: Coxcombry Cox"comb`ry (-r?), n. The manners of a coxcomb; foppishness.

coxswain.c: Coxswain Cox"swain` (k?k"sw?n, Colloq. k?k"s'n), n. See Cockswain.

coy.c: Coy Coy (koi), a. [OE. coi quiet, still, OF. coi, coit, fr.L. quietus quiet, p. p. of quiescere to rest, quie rest; prob. akin to E. while. See While, and cf. Quiet, Quit, Quite.] 1. Quiet; still. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Coy Coy, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Coyed (koid); p. pr. & vb. n. Coying.] 1. To allure; to entice; to decoy. [Obs.]
Coy Coy, v. i. 1. To behave with reserve or coyness; to shrink from approach or familiarity. [Obs.]

coyish.c: Coyish Coy"ish, a. Somewhat coy or reserved. Warner.

coyly.c: Coyly Coy"ly, adv. In a coy manner; with reserve.

coyness.c: Coyness Coy"ness, n. The quality of being coy; feigned o? bashful unwillingness to become familiar; reserve.

coyote.c: Coyote Coy"o*te (k?"?-t? or k?"?t), n. [Spanish Amer., fr. Mexican coyotl.] (Zool.) A carnivorous animal (Canis latrans), allied to the dog, found in the western part of North America; -- called also prairie wolf. Its voice is a snapping bark, followed by a prolonged, shrill howl.
Coyote State Coyote State. South Dakota; -- a nickname.

coyotillo.c: Coyotillo ‖Co`yo*til"lo (?), n. [Mex. Sp. dim. See Coyote.] A low rhamnaceous shrub (Karwinskia humboldtiana) of the southwestern United States and Mexico. Its berries are said to be poisonous to the coyote.

coypu.c: Coypu ‖Coy"pu (koi"p??), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A South American rodent (Myopotamus coypus), allied to the beaver. It produces a valuable fur called nutria. [Written also coypou.]

coz.c: Coz Coz (kŭz), n. A contraction of cousin. Shak.

cozen.c: Cozen Coz"en (k?z"'n), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cozened (-'nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Cozening (-'n-?ng). ] [From cousin, hence, literally, to deceive through pretext of relationship, F. cousiner.] To cheat; to defraud; to beguile; to deceive, usually by small arts, or in a pitiful way.
Cozen Coz"en, v. i. To deceive; to cheat; to act deceitfully.

cozenage.c: Cozenage Coz"en*age (-aj), n. [See Cozen, and cf. Cousinage.] The art or practice of cozening; artifice; fraud. Shak.

cozener.c: Cozener Coz"en*er (k?z"'n-?r), n. One who cheats or defrauds.

coziness.c: Coziness Co"zi*ness, n. The state or quality of being cozy.

cozy.c: Cozy Co"zy (k?"z?), a. [Compar. Cozier (-z?-?r); superl. Coziest.] [Cf. Scot. cosie, cozie, prob. from Gael. cosach abounding in hollows, or cosagach full of holes or crevices, snug, sheltered, from cos a hollow, a crevice.]
Cozy Co"zy, n. [See Cozy,a.] A wadded covering, often decorative, for a teakettle or other vessel to keep the contents hot. Also called tea cozy

crab.c: Crab Crab (krăb), n. [AS. crabba; akin to D. krab, G. krabbe, krebs, Icel. krabbi, Sw. krabba, Dan. krabbe, and perh. to E. cramp. Cf. Crawfish.] 1. (Zool.) One of the brachyuran Crustacea. They are mostly marine, and usually have a broad, short body, covered with a strong shell or carapace. The abdomen is small and curled up beneath the body.
Crab Crab (krăb), v. t. 1. To make sour or morose; to embitter. [Obs.]
Crab Crab, v. i. (Naut.)To drift sidewise or to leeward, as a vessel. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
Crab Crab, a. [Prob. from the same root as crab, n.] Sour; rough; austere.
Crab tree Crab" tree (trē`). See under Crab.

crabbed.c: Crabbed Crab"bed (kr?b"b?d), a. [See Crab,n.] 1. Characterized by or manifesting, sourness, peevishness, or moroseness; harsh; cross; cynical; -- applied to feelings, disposition, or manners.

crabber.c: Crabber Crab"ber (kr?b"b?r), n. One who catches crabs.

crabbing.c: Crabbing Crab"bing, n. 1. The act or art of catching crabs.

crabbish.c: Crabbish Crab"bish (krăb"bĭsh), a. Somewhat sour or cross.

crabby.c: Crabby Crab"by (-by̆), a. Crabbed; difficult, or perplexing. “Persius is crabby, because ancient.” Marston.

crabeater.c: Crabeater Crab"eat`er (krăb"ēt`ẽr), n. (Zool.) (a) The cobia. (b) An etheostomoid fish of the southern United States (Hadropterus nigrofasciatus). (c) A small European heron (Ardea minuta, and other allied species).

craber.c: Craber Cra"ber (krā"bẽr), n. (Zool.) The water rat. Walton.

crabfaced.c: Crabfaced Crab"faced` (krăb"fāst`), a. Having a sour, disagreeable countenance. Beau. & Fl.

crabsidle.c: Crabsidle Crab"si`dle (-sī`d'l), v. i. To move sidewise, as a crab. [Jocular]. Southey.

crabstick.c: Crabstick Crab"stick` (-stĭk`), n. A stick, cane, or cudgel, made of the wood of the crab tree.

crabyaws.c: Crab-yaws Crab"-yaws` (kr?b"y?z`), n. (Med.) A disease in the West Indies. It is a kind of ulcer on the soles of the feet, with very hard edges. See Yaws. Dunglison.

crack.c: Crack Crack (krăk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cracked (krăkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Cracking.] [OE. cracken, craken, to crack, break, boast, AS. cracian, cearcian, to crack; akin to D. kraken, G. krachen; cf. Skr. garj to rattle, or perh. of imitative origin. Cf. Crake, Cracknel, Creak.]
Crack Crack, v. i. 1. To burst or open in chinks; to break, with or without quite separating into parts.
Crack Crack, n. 1. A partial separation of parts, with or without a perceptible opening; a chink or fissure; a narrow breach; a crevice; as, a crack in timber, or in a wall, or in glass.
Crack Crack, a. Of superior excellence; having qualities to be boasted of; as, a crack shot. [Colloq.]

crackajack.c: Crackajack Crack"a*jack` (?), n. [Now usually spelled crackerjack.] [prob. from crack + jack, a man.] 1. An individual of marked ability or excellence, esp. in some sport; as, he is a crackajack at tennis. [Slang]
Crackajack Crack"a*jack`, a. [Now usually spelled crackerjack.] Of marked ability or excellence. [Slang]

crackbrained.c: Crack-brained crackbrained crackbrained, Crack"-brained` (-brānd`), a. Having an impaired intellect; whimsical; extremely foolish; crazy; as, crackbrained notions. Pope.

cracked.c: Cracked Cracked (krăkt), a. 1. Coarsely ground or broken; as, cracked wheat.

cracker.c: Cracker Crack"er (krăk"ẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, cracks.
Cracker State Cracker State. Georgia; -- a nickname. See Cracker, n. 5.

crackerjack.c: Crackerjack Crack"er*jack` (?), n. [also spelled crackerjack.] [prob. from crack + jack, a man.] 1. An individual of marked ability or excellence, esp. in some sport; as, he is a crackajack at tennis. [Slang]
Crackerjack Crack"er*jack`, a. [also spelled crackajack.] Of marked ability or excellence. [Slang]

crackle.c: Crackle Crac"kle (krăk"k'l), v. i. [Dim. of crack.] To make slight cracks; to make small, sharp, sudden noises, rapidly or frequently repeated; to crepitate; as, burning thorns crackle.
Crackle Crac"kle, n. 1. The noise of slight and frequent cracks or reports; a crackling.

crackled.c: Crackled Crac"kled (-k'ld), a. (Fine Arts) Covered with minute cracks in the glaze; -- said of some kinds of porcelain and fine earthenware.

crackling.c: Crackling Crac"kling (kr?k"kl?ng), n. 1. The making of small, sharp cracks or reports, frequently repeated.

crackaloo.c: Crackaloo Crack-loo { Crack"-loo` (?), n. Also Crack"a*loo` }. A kind of gambling game consisting in pitching coins to or towards the ceiling of a room so that they shall fall as near as possible to a certain crack in the floor. [Gamblers' Cant, U. S.]

cracknel.c: Cracknel Crack"nel (kr?k"n?l), n. [F. craquelin, fr. D. krakeling, fr. krakken to crack. See Crack, v. t.] A hard brittle cake or biscuit. Spenser.

cracksman.c: Cracksman Cracks"man (kr?ks"man), n., pl. Cracksmen (-men). A burglar. [Slang]

cracovian.c: Cracovian Cra*co"vi*an (kr?-k?"v?-an), a. Of or pertaining to Cracow in Poland.

cracovienne.c: Cracovienne ‖Cra*co`vi*enne" (kr?-k?`v?-?n"), n. [F., fr. Cracow, the city.] (Mus.) A lively Polish dance, in 2-4 time.

cracowes.c: Cracowes Cra"cowes (kr?"k?z), n. pl. Long-toed boots or shoes formerly worn in many parts of Europe; -- so called from Cracow, in Poland, where they were first worn in the fourteenth century. Fairholt.

cradle.c: Cradle Cra"dle (krād'l), n. [AS. cradel, cradol, prob. from Celtic; cf. Gael. creathall, Ir. craidhal, W. cryd a shaking or rocking, a cradle; perh. akin to E. crate.] 1. A bed or cot for a baby, oscillating on rockers or swinging on pivots; hence, the place of origin, or in which anything is nurtured or protected in the earlier period of existence; as, a cradle of crime; the cradle of liberty.
Cradle Cra"dle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Cradled (-d'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Cradling (-dl?ng).] 1. To lay to rest, or rock, as in a cradle; to lull or quiet, as by rocking.
Cradle Cra"dle, v. i. To lie or lodge, as in a cradle.

cradleland.c: Cradleland Cra"dle*land` (krā"d'l*lănd`), n. Land or region where one was cradled; hence, land of origin.

cradling.c: Cradling Cra"dling (-dl?ng), n. 1. The act of using a cradle.

craft.c: Craft Craft (krȧft), n. [AS. cræft strength, skill, art, cunning; akin to OS., G., Sw., & Dan. kraft strength, D. kracht, Icel. kraptr; perh. originally, a drawing together, stretching, from the root of E. cramp.] 1. Strength; might; secret power. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Craft Craft, v. t. To play tricks; to practice artifice. [Obs.]

craftily.c: Craftily Craft"i*ly (-?-l?), adv. [See Crafty.] With craft; artfully; cunningly.

craftiness.c: Craftiness Craft"i*ness (kr?ft"?-n?s), n. Dexterity in devising and effecting a purpose; cunning; artifice; stratagem.

craftless.c: Craftless Craft"less (-l?s), a. Without craft or cunning.

craftsman.c: Craftsman Crafts"man (kr?fts"man), n.; pl. Craftsmen (-men). One skilled in some trade or manual occupation; an artificer; a mechanic.

craftsmanship.c: Craftsmanship Crafts"man*ship, n. The work of a craftsman.

craftsmaster.c: Craftsmaster Crafts"mas`ter (-m?s`t?r), n. One skilled in his craft or trade; one of superior cunning.

crafty.c: Crafty Craft"y (kr?ft"?), a. [AS. cræftig.] 1. Relating to, or characterized by, craft or skill; dexterous. [Obs.] “Crafty work.” Piers Plowman.

crag.c: Crag Crag (krăg), n. [W. craig; akin to Gael. creag, Corn. karak, Armor. karrek.] 1. A steep, rugged rock; a rough, broken cliff, or point of a rock, on a ledge.
Crag Crag, n. [A form of craw: cf. D. kraag neck, collar, G. kragen. See Craw.] 1. The neck or throat [Obs.]

cragged.c: Cragged Crag"ged (-gĕd), a. Full of crags, or steep, broken rocks; abounding with prominences, points, and inequalities; rough; rugged.

craggedness.c: Craggedness Crag"ged*ness, n. The quality or state of being cragged; cragginess.

cragginess.c: Cragginess Crag"gi*ness (-g?-n?s), n. The state of being craggy.

craggy.c: Craggy Crag"gy (krăg"gy̆), a. Full of crags; rugged with projecting points of rocks; as, the craggy side of a mountain. “The craggy ledge.” Tennyson.

cragsman.c: Cragsman Crags"man (krăgz"main), n.; pl. Cragsmen (-mein). One accustomed to climb rocks or crags; esp., one who makes a business of climbing the cliffs overhanging the sea to get the eggs of sea birds or the birds themselves.

craig.c: Craig flounder Craig" floun`der (krāg" floun`dẽr). [Scot. craig a rock. See 1st Crag.] (Zool.) The pole flounder.

crail.c: Crail Crail (krāl), n. [See Creel.] A creel or osier basket.

crake.c: Crake Crake (krāk), v. t. & i. [See Crack.] 1. To cry out harshly and loudly, like the bird called crake.
Crake Crake, n. A boast. See Crack, n. [Obs.] Spenser.

Crake Crake, n. [Cf. Icel. krāka crow, krākr raven, Sw. kråka, Dan. krage; perh. of imitative origin. Cf. Crow.] (Zool.) Any species or rail of the genera Crex and Porzana; -- so called from its singular cry. See Corncrake.

craker.c: Craker Crak"er (kr?k"?r), n. One who boasts; a braggart. [Obs.] Old Play.

cram.c: Cram Cram (krăm), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Crammed (krămd); p. pr. & vb. n. Cramming.] [AS. crammian to cram; akin to Icel. kremja to squeeze, bruise, Sw. krama to press. Cf. Cramp.] 1.
